speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise pursuant to Standing Order 43 to present a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. The weekend resignation of Air Canada vice-president Yves Menard amid conflict of interest charges, the previous widespread knowledge of his holdings among Air Canada officials, the frequent reports of other conflicts of interest such as that involving Air Canada's Skifari package to Jasper and the telegram sent this morning to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) from 73 Air Canada revenue accounting employees demanding an investigation into Air Canada, as well as the previous but constant reports of managerial disarray, low employee morale, directors' meetings held in Florida, and the unique in-Canada deficit incurred by Air Canada this year, are reasons why the House has no alternative but to support this motion for the sake of our national airline's future. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Portage (Mr. Masniuk):
That the House direct the Acting Prime Minister to initiate an immediate independent inquiry into the entire operation of the Air Canada Crown corporation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a motion of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. I wish to say that had it not been for the twelve noon deadline set by the House and the delay in issuing Statistics Canada figures, which confirm that the economy has slipped into a recession, I would have moved this motion under Standing Order 26 for debate.
However, in light of the GNP figures released today which show there has been a decline of 1.3 per cent in real growth in the fourth quarter of 1974 resulting in a standstill year in growth for Canada, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Central Nova:
That this House instruct the federal government to exercise its mandate of responsible leadership promised to the Canadian people in the last election and that the Minister of Finance make a statement on motions on the status of Canada's economy and immediately initiate preparations for the introduction of a new budget which would more effectively counteract the current economic slump.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a point of order in relation to the catastrophe which has developed in the grain industry caused by the current strikes at Vancouver. The situation is past the stage where it matters who is wrong and who is right. Canada's reputation as a reliable grain supplier has been severely damaged and the Canadian Wheat Board is contemplating either limiting sales or cancelling overseas delivery orders.
I believe the government House leader has a responsibility to the Canadian people to put forward emergency legislation placing the grain workers involved in the strikes at the West Coast back at work. I do not necessarily like this method of settling a labour dispute, but the situation at Vancouver is so serious that I believe this kind of action is warranted.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Acting Prime Minister having to do with the construction of a gas pipeline from the north. May I ask the Acting Prime Minister whether what I am quoting still represents government policy. On July 19, 1973 the then minister of Indian affairs and northern development, now President of the Treasury Board, said in evidence in the appropriate House committee:
As Minister of Northern Development, I am responsible for granting a right of way in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. Under the Territorial Lands Act I can hold hearings. And before I give to any group a right of way to build a pipeline, I shall have public hearings to assess the social and environmental impact on the construction of a pipeline in the north.
Is that still the policy of the government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerard Pelletier (Minister of Communications) moved
subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH COMMISSION
speechtext:
that Bill C-5, to establish the Canadian Radiotelevision and Telecommunications Commission, to amend the Broadcasting Act and other acts in consequence thereof and to enact other consequential provisions, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to introduce for consideration by hon. members a bill establishing the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission.
The regulation of communications at the federal level is carried out, at the present time, by two separate agencies: The Canadian Radio-Television Commission as regards Broadcasting including cable Television and the Telecommunication Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission as regards telephone and telegraph carriers. Hon. members of this House probably know that the principal telephone and telegraph carriers now under the jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada and, consequently, of the CTC, are: Bell Canada, which operates its telephone network in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and in parts of the Northwest Territories. The corporation has, moreover, been declared to be a "work for the general advantage of Canada", as they say in proper legal jargon.
British Columbia Telephone Limited which also has been declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada, and, finally, CN-CP Telecommunications, which operate a public telegraph network throughout Canada and which, in competition with other telephone companies, offer various types of private services. They have also installed a microwave long distance network parallel to the network of the Trans-Canada Telephone System.
Hon. members are also aware that since 1968 the Canadian Radio-television Commission has been responsible for issuing the licences for the operation of Broadcasting stations, whether they are privately owned or are part of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation networks. The commission, consisting of five full time members and ten part time members, is more particularly responsible for the implementation of the broadcasting policy for Canada enunciated in section 3 of the Broadcasting Act. It has to take the necessary steps to ensure that broadcasting should serve to safe-guarding and enriching Canadian culture in all its aspects. Another objective of the commission is to provide, by means of broadcasting, transmitting and receiving stations, high quality service in both official languages. This government is determined to uphold the broadcasting policy approved by Parliament in 1968 and will continue to support all the efforts of the regulatory agency and others concerned with the implementation of that policy.
The essential purpose of this bill is to entrust the regulation of all federally-regulated telecommunications to a

single agency to be known in future as the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission- thus retaining the acronym CRTC-to emphasize the significance which this government sees in both aspects of telecommunications, namely broadcasting an transmission. The integration of the different modes of telecommunication, whether they are telephone, broadcasting, coaxial cable or microwave, becomes more and more complete every day. The advent of cable television, with its still undeveloped two-way potential, has made it imperative to entrust the different aspects of telecommunications to a single regulatory agency in order to ensure the harmonious development of these new techniques, in a manner compatible with the best interests of Canadian citizens.
This bill is but the first step towards the modernization of the federal statutes relating to telecommunications. In the near future, the government intends to submit to Parliament the second phase of this Legislative project. This will entail an in-depth revision of the provisions of the Railway Act applying to telephone and telegraph, of the Telegraphs Act, of the Radio Act, and of the Broadcasting Act. The Acts incorporating the Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Corporation, and Telesat Act will also be amended.
Before introducing this second bill to Parliament, the government wishes to ascertain the views of the provincial Governments on the most effective methods of regulating telecommunications. By so doing, we hope, Mr. Speaker, to obtain a better understanding of the various factors and elements to be taken into account in drafting our second stage of legislation. The positions of the federal government have already been published in a green paper intitled "Proposals for a Telecommunications Policy for Canada", which was tabled in the House of Commons in April 1973. This exchange of views with the provinces becomes all the more necessary in the light of the present division of responsibilities in the field of telecommunications; Parliament has exclusive legislative authority over radiocommunications, including broadcasting which television in turn includes cable, while the provincial legislatures control local telephone or telegraph indertak-ings, the great majority of which have not been declared to be "works" for the general advantage of Canada. It is therefore desirable, perhaps even essential, to achieve as soon as possible a better coordination of governmental efforts in this regard and of the initiatives of the several regulatory agencies in order to provide all Canadians in all parts of the country with the telecommunications and broadcasting services they have a right to expect.
In November 1973, a conference of ministers responsible for communications was held in Ottawa. At that time, I informed the provincial ministers of our intention to introduce the present bill merging the two federal agencies directly responsible for regulating telecommunications, without in any way changing existing powers over the undertakings respectively subject to their authority. The commission will continue, until after the enactment of the second legislative measure, to exercise the present powers of the CRTC over broadcasting undertakings. The new commission will also apply the provisions of the Railway Act and the National Transportation Act to the telephone and telegraph companies. With regard to regula-
March 4, 1975

tory principles and procedures, this merger will obviously lead to better coordination and greater unity of thought.
The Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission will consist of a maximum of nine full time members and ten part time members. The existing CRTC comprises five full time members and ten part time members. The increased responsibilities of the new commission account for the proposed appointment of four additional full time members to help the commission in adequately fulfilling its mandate. When the act is put into force, all the members of the CRTC will become members of the new commission until their respective terms of office expire.
The bill also provides for the transfer to the new commission, when the act is put into force, of matters that are presently dealt with by the CRTC, with the exception of those matters that may already be the subject of a hearing or of an inquiry at that time which will be decided by the present commission and the CTC. The governor in council will nonetheless be authorized to depart from this rule if it is unrealistic to defer unduly the assumption by the commission of certain matters that may be the subject of a hearing or of an inquiry. In these cases, steps will be taken to protect the rights of the parties concerned and of the general public.
This act will be put into force by proclamation. The delay between the enactment of this legislation and its implementation will enable the government to set up the administrative structures required to ensure the smooth running of the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission. This act will permit better coordination of telecommunications regulatory policy at the federal level. This rearrangement of administrative structures, as I have already mentioned, is only the first manifestation of our desire to integrate the various components of telecommunication in the best interests of all Canadians. The government is convinced that it will enable the members of the new commission to work in a more adequate and sustained way toward the supervision of the national broadcasting and telecommunication networks.

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the principle of the legislation before the House, in so far as it constitutes an attempt to consolidate under the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier), a single federal regulatory agency covering the whole field of telecommunications and the exercise of authority over both the CBC and the operations of the federally-regulated telecommunications carriers, is correct. A detailed analysis of the legislation exposes weaknesses and anomalies which, however, it would be more appropriate to discuss in committee. We intend to do this at the appropriate time and in the appropriate manner, and we hope we will be able to put forth constructive amendments for the minister's consideration and, I trust, acceptance and implementation.
I propose, today, to discuss in a more general way my party's view of Canadian communications policy generally, to indicate the particular areas where wrong policy directions have in our view been taken, and to direct the
Broadcasting
attention of the minister and the House to policy failures which, if allowed to continue uncorrected, will create very serious problems for Canadians generally. Perhaps the most serious general criticism that can be levelled at this government is its apparent unwillingness and failure to enter into meaningful negotiations with its provincial counterparts in connection with the jurisdictional jungle that over the years has developed in relation to communications matters.
Our party believes that the time has long since passed when a national communications policy should be set in place. We believe that such a national communications policy should have certain specific objectives, including that of protecting and promoting the political, social and economic fibre of Canada. It should contribute to the flow and exchange of regional and cultural information and the development of national unity. It should reflect Canadian identity and, as well, the diversity of Canadian culture and social values. And, generally, it should facilitate the orderly development of telecommunications in Canada, for Canadians, and the provision of efficient and economical systems and services to all Canadians at rates which are just and reasonable.
Clearly, a first and fundamental step in putting in place such a policy would be to resolve with the provinces the competing and conflicting jurisdictional claims between broadcasters, cable operators, common carriers and governments themselves. We should recognize, without equivocation, that the constitutional straitjacket imposed on telecommunications at the time of confederation, rigidly and jealously exercised by successive federal governments, is no longer an appropriate answer in this era of technological change. Instead, the federal government should define the national interest in telecommunications with the sense of urgency, imagination and initiative which the matter deserves.
With this objective in mind, we would propose that certain specific steps be taken, namely, consolidating under the Minister of Communications the present eight different federal statutes relating to telecommunications; the establishment of one federal authority to regulate standards for systems and equipment; federal recognition that the provinces should participate in the regulation of telecommunications through a Canadian communications commission composed of federal and provincial nominees to replace and carry out the duties proposed to be carried out by the commission established by the legislation before us, and with corresponding technical subcommittees for the industrial components falling under its jurisdiction. It would, and should be, a cornerstone of federal communications policy that the federal government recognize the paramountcy of provincial communications systems in place and put an end to the jurisdictional wrangling in existence or in process which at this point in time characterizes the communications mess presently gripping our country.
In order to stimulate research, long-range and coordinated planning and to publicly review the work and activities of the Canadian communications commission, we believe the government should establish a communications council with a permanent secretariat founded by, but

independent of, the government with a mandate to report at least once a year to the people of Canada on the state and scope of telecommunications in this country.
That, very briefly, puts before the House a communications policy in specific terms as an alternative to the present chaotic situation characterized by green papers, white papers and piecemeal legislation and jurisdictional struggles which can only further exacerbate the sense of regional alienation and chronic confrontation which seems to characterize federal-provincial relations under this government.
The specific, fundamental, unanswered question in communications policy in this country is simply this: what role does the federal government see provincial governments playing in the communications field?
Has the province of Saskatchewan negotiated a special arrangement for the operation of cable television within its borders? If so, what are the terms of the arrangement, and are similar arrangements being negotiated with other provinces which may desire them? There is little to be lost, and perhaps everything to be gained, in the development of a broadcasting and, in particular, cable regulatory framework in which provinces have a legitimate role. The participation of provincial Crown corporations or agents in the field of broadcasting and cable origination, transmission of programs and programming within over-all guidelines established by the federal government, could be of great advantage. Such a policy approach permits provinces to participate in the control of what to many is an important or vital aspect of their culture and way of life.
This concern by provincial governments across the country from the viewpoint of mass media represents a legitimate concern for responsible diversity. As with other mass media ownership, it would be perhaps unwise to concentrate ownership or program control in any one set of hands. Nevertheless, within an appropriate framework established in the interests of each and all, provincial partnership and participation in this field should be welcome.
There can be little doubt, either, that it would be desirable to openly modify present government policy and permit, if not encourage, educational institutions and agents of Her Majesty in right of any province, not excluding municipal or other public bodies, to participate appropriately in broadcasting and programming endeavours. This should be within co-ordinating federal regulations establishing minimum requirements, providing also that the broadcast licensee shall be free of direct political control.
The bill we have before us may appear routine and purely functional, but I believe that a certain degree of policy formulation lies beneath the surface. The Minister of Communications has attempted in the past to pass off the intent of the bill and to allay the fears of provincial ministers of communications. He portrays it as the merging of two regulating bodies, an internal reshuffle of regulatory agencies of the federal government that brings no change whatsoever to the respective authorities nor to the administrative dispositions between the provinces and the federal government as regards the regulation of telecommunications. Yet the minister knows that this is not altogether an accurate portrayal of the facts.

The provincial ministers have, in fact, been making representations to the federal Minister of Communications seeking some kind of resolution to the long-standing struggle over communications jurisdiction. The bill before us, I point out, is another step toward solidifying the federal government's position vis-a-vis the provinces without their consent or consultation. The provincial ministers' conference in Quebec City in 1972 resulted in the federal government being accused of duplicating provincial telecommunications systems in licensing the CN-CP telecommunications' network. The provinces' communications ministers' conference in 1973 pleaded with Ottawa to stay out of provincial areas of jurisdiction. The provinces reacted to the federal green paper on communications released in 1974 by reiterating that in their view the regulation of telephone rates was a matter solely within provincial jurisdiction.
The minister admits openly that the number of court proceedings is increasing in which federal-provincial communications jurisdiction is the basic issue. Amid this turmoil, the minister simply hides behind that old line of defence, the constitution. "Conflicts of jurisdiction are not the business of federal-provincial ministers' conferences. That comes under the jurisdiction of a constitutional conference or the courts"-that is what the minister said. Why then, I might ask, would the minister choose to buttress his stand against the provinces by unilaterally increasing the ambit of the CRTC while there are existing provincial administrations for dealing with some of the problems in which the federal government has become involved? Why will the minister not consent to further federal-provincial conferences on the matter?
Federal and provincial interests in telecommunications can, and should be, complementary rather than conflicting, and afford ample opportunity for constructive cooperation by all levels of government in Canada. Given the great ambiguity in the determination of jurisdiction for communications and cable TV, it is entirely reasonable for provinces to seek to play an effective role in this sector. The provinces have very real interests and concerns relating to their exclusive powers. Given the present rigidity of the government, and given also the June 4, 1970, government directive to the CRTC to exclude provinces or their agents, it is not surprising that a federal-provincial confrontation is shaping up. Flexibility and reasonableness, combined with a willingness to participate in meaningful federal-provincial discussions, are required.
For the future, as in the present, the importance of telecommunications to the provinces and the federal government requires co-operation and good will. Not satisfactory are back-door responses in contradiction to the federal government's own directive, for example the CRTC allowing the Quebec Deposit and Investment Fund, a provincial Crown agent, to become a major shareholder in a cable TV company. Provincial participation is perhaps desirable, but the federal government should admit it for what it is.
The future course of this vital telecommunications and communications sector should be founded on the decisions of reasonable men working together, whether they be at the federal or provincial level, and the conclusions and

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the advent in recent years of satellites and computers has led to a revolution in the whole field of communications. That revolution has had very serious effects in this country, to a large extent because of the divided jurisdiction between the federal and provincial governments. This has made it increasingly difficult to know precisely who has not only the right but the responsibility for determining what communications policy will be and what charges we will make for different methods of communication.
Similarly, the advent of cable television has created a great deal of contention and division of opinion between the federal government, which claims to have the right to regulate radio and television, and the provinces which, because of their concern with educational matters, feel they must have a great deal of say-not the whole say- about the form of transmission of information which can, and probably will be-if it is not already-one of the most important methods of getting education to the people in all age groups. For this reason there is now, and has been for some time-as the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Balfour) has already said-a great deal of conflict between the provinces and the federal government about where, in fact, rests the right to regulate. My colleague the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) will deal with that question.
I want to deal with one of the main tasks which, if I understood the minister correctly, has been the responsibility of the Canadian Transport Commission-and, much earlier, the responsibility of the Board of Transport Commissioners-but which will, if we pass this measure, become the responsibility of the CRTC in its new form. To the extent that the responsibility for setting telephone rates is taken from the present Canadian Transport Commission and given to the CRTC, we in this party will support that proposal because the fact is-and I want to take a few minutes to place some examples on the record- that the record of the CTC has been one of complete failure. It has never, so far as I can find out, turned down a single application made to it by Bell Canada for permission to increase rates. On the other hand, the CRTC has been an active, aggressive, socially conscious organization which has in the field, so far as it has responsibility, done a good deal of research into the basic problems, has consulted with the public, has engaged in dialogue with the public and with interested organizations and has tried to chart a policy which would be of benefit to the people as a whole. This does not mean I agree with every decision made by the CRTC, but at least it has seemed to take its responsibility seriously. To that extent we can support the change the minister is proposing.
Having said that, I want to remind the minister of a judgment of Mr. Justice William Douglas of the United States Supreme Court, as set out in his autobiography, in which he discusses his experience as chairman of the United States Securities and Exchange Commission during the middle thirties. He makes the suggestion that no regulatory agency should be permitted to exist for more
Broadcasting
than ten years, because after ten years the agency which has been established to regulate and monitor the companies and corporations in the field for which it has been given responsibility inevitably finds that it becomes the servant of those companies and corporations rather than the regulatory agency or the master which tells them what to do. I think this happens almost inevitably in respect of every regulatory agency which has been established not only in Canada but in every other country.
I wish to take a few moments to place on the record what has happened in respect of the supposed regulation of telephone rates in the area in which the federal government has responsibility-Ontario and Quebec. If one examines the record of the Canadian Transport Commission, one finds that in every case over the years in which Bell Canada has asked for a rate increase, that rate increase has been granted. In every case where Bell Canada received an increase and the board took the time and trouble not merely to grant the increase but to indicate what it believed would be a fair rate of return for Bell Canada, we find that when the company came back one year, two years or three years later to ask for another increase, in fact the rate of return the company had received was not the rate of return the regulatory agency had said it should have, but was more than that. But despite that, the principle laid down by the regulatory agency was overlooked by the agency and a further increase was granted.
If one looks at the record from 1958 to the middle 1960s, one sees that Bell Canada consistently exceeded the level of earnings established by the old Board of Transport Commissioners. The excess profits of Bell Canada, which I suggest were illegal and in violation of the board's own rulings, amounted to about $37 million. In 1964 the board conducted a further investigation of the pricing procedures of Bell Canada, but rather than directing its attention to the excessive profit level, the board concerned itself merely with the application by Bell to change its permissible level of profits in order to justify a rate increase.
In 1966 the board raised the permissible level of Bell Canada's earnings to fall within the range of between 6.2 per cent and 6.6 per cent of the total average capitalization. A year later Bell came back for another increase. It was then found that the rate of return had not remained in the 6.2 per cent to 6.6 per cent range which the board had authorized, but in fact had reached 6.8 per cent. In 1968 it was up to 6.9 per cent. The board, however, gave Bell another increase. Having been encouraged by the CTC's lack of resolve in the face of pressure, Bell Canada came back in 1969 to ask for a new profit level of 8 per cent to 9 per cent return on total capital. On that occasion the board avoided its responsibility and refused to fix any permissible level. The result was that Bell increased its net earnings by almost $12 Vi million in 1969 over 1968. By this time it had been able to earn a return on equity of 7.3 per cent.
The 1969 judgment was delivered in September, and in June of 1970 Bell Canada was back with a further application to the CTC for a revised rate structure designed to increase its revenue by $30 million. The company obtained another increase. In 1971 Bell Canada was back again, despite the increase in 1970. This time it wished an

increase that would permit it to have a return of not less than 8.2 per cent, ranging up to 9 per cent, on capital. The CTC disagreed and limited the additional revenue to $47.2 million, which it estimated would give a return on total average capital of 7.8 per cent and 9.5 per cent on common equity. That was in 1971. In 1972 Bell Canada was back again asking for a very sharp increase. The CTC agreed to that. They never once turned down an application for a rate increase. They never once said to Bell Telephone, "We gave you an increase; you exceeded the profitability level which we set and we are not going to give you another increase." They never once took the step which United States regulatory agencies have taken in the past and said, in effect, "You have already exceeded the profitability level for which you asked and which we allowed, so for the month of September", or whatever the month may be, "you should not charge your customers anything; you should give them a free month because you have already exceeded the rate which we allowed".
But, of course, the Canadian regulatory agency could not do that: that would be too much in the interest of the consumer, and the last person the CTC thinks about is the Canadian consumer.
So Bell Canada asked for an increase in 1972. Unfortunately for them, in 1972 this country had a minority government. The government of the day knew that if it permitted an increase in rates to Bell Canada, it-the government-might not survive. So for the first and only time the government suspended the rate increase which had been asked for by Bell Canada and approved by CTC. The government said it was suspending a telephone rate increase for Bell Canada partly to ensure that at least basic communications services were available to all Canadians, wherever they lived, at just and reasonable rates. That was in a period when we had a minority government, in 1973. But by 1974 the election was over, we no longer had a minority government and the government did not have to worry about it. Therefore, the government permitted an increase in the way it had always permitted increases in the past, despite the recommendations of a number of organizations and with no intervention from the regulatory agency.
Recommendations were made to the minister by a number of organizations which were concerned about the effect of the increases on consumers. I have before me some of the submissions which were made to the minister. An organization called Action Bell Canada made a submission to the minister in which they pointed out the contradictions and inadequacies in the CTC decision. I want to put on record some of the arguments which they put forward-arguments, incidentally, which were completely ignored and never reviewed by the government when it permitted Bell Canada the increase for which it had asked. Action Bell Canada said, among other things:
The CTC has given Bell Canada millions of dollars by almost totally accepting Bell's arguments (or amended Application B. This has been done without Bell Canada even presenting its total profit picture to the commission or the CTC really knowing exactly how much it is giving away. Indeed, Bell Canada's chairman indicated in the hearing that this company may be back shortly for more money from the CTC.

I am reasonably certain that before 1975 is over, Bell Canada will be back. After all, why should they miss this year when they have not missed a year in the last ten? Action Bell Canada said, further:
The amended Application B decision continually shows CTC's disenchantment with the token public participation methods it grudgingly adopted. CTC hits out at those new intervenors who misunderstand CTC regulation protocol and who the CTC labels as social impact intervenors. Instead of direct input from consumer groups in reforming its procedures, the CTC opts for an independent legal counsel to represent the public interest. The commission also proposes that Bell Canada's internal customer studies underway, along with future government studies on the social responsiveness of telephone service, will go a long way towards eliminating frustrations among Bell customers.
One of the things which is obvious to anyone who makes the most cursory examination of Bell's applications and interventions is that consumers and their organizations are virtually powerless to make a real presentation because Bell's organization is so large and its system so complicated that the costs of really studying it are so great that none of the organizations which have shown interest are able financially, or in terms of personnel, to do the job required. The fact is that in the most recent application which was approved, the Consumers' Association of Canada refused to make a real submission, not because they did not want to, not because they did not think that the rate increase being asked for by Bell was unjustified but simply because they did not have the money required. They calculated that it would cost at least $20,000 just to get a lawyer to represent them. What it would have cost to get engineering and accounting technical advice which they would have required, I certainly do not know, but we are probably talking in terms of $100,000 or more. The Consumers' Association of Canada simply did not have that kind of money.
The CTC said, "Because organizations cannot come forward with real technical briefs, because they just argue on the basis of social impact, and so on, we are not really very interested in their submissions because they have nothing really worth-while to contribute to the hearings". Instead of the CTC doing the job itself, or ensuring that the government would supply the technical know-how to interested organizations, the CTC said, in effect, that they were not able to do the job themselves and they did not really want to hear from these organizations in the future. Having said that, the CTC itself got into social impact rulings. Action Bell Canada said, further:
It would allow 10 cent pay-phones at sidewalk locations but not at citizen group locations and exemptions to directory assistance charges to those 65 and over only if they come to Bell and make such a request. The commission can accept Bell arguments for reduced rates for large customers having the Telpak service while not accepting intervenors' requests for the abolition of security deposits that mainly affect the poor.
It is a long-standing complaint on the part of subscribers in Ontario and Quebec that they are required to put down a security deposit-I cannot at the moment remember whether it is $25 or $35-but it is money which stays with Bell Canada and which they use interest-free for their own purposes. Action Bell Canada continues:
CTC sees nothing wrong with semi-automatic price increases through upgroupings in the larger centres of Toronto and Montreal this year at an additional 60 cents a month per subscriber, yet it is willing to take a temporary stand on the abolition of the rate classification for the smallest telephone exchanges.
March 4, 1975

I could speak at length on the representations which were made to the minister, but let me conclude by saying that the minister simply ignored those representations and allowed the rate increase requested by Bell Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I have already said that in our view, giving the job of regulating rates to the CRTC and taking it away from the CTC cannot be anything but an improvement. There is certainly no agency in existence, or contemplated, which could do a worse job than the CTC or the Board of Transport Commissioners before it. Having said that, it seems to me that if parliament does not first ask itself what the objectives are which we set in the provision of telephone service, we tie the hands of the agency which is supposed to regulate the rates, so that we cannot do a job-because if it is our intention to provide telephone service to all Canadian citizens who want that service, there is one approach, namely, that we tell the regulatory agency what the objective is and then try to implement that objective. We believe that should be the objective.
Just as we now say that every person is entitled to adequate housing, education and health standards, we say that in this modern age every person should be provided with telephone service. If that is said, the question is approached from one point of view. If, on the other hand, we say-as we seem to be saying in the way in which people are provided with telephones in parts of Ontario, Quebec and the territories-that in the providing of telephone service an important aspect shall be that the private investors shall make a reasonable profit, whatever that may be, then of course the provision of service is an entirely different matter. We believe that once that is done-that is what we have done in Ontario and Quebec for many years and it is what this government obviously expects to continue-the job of the regulatory agency is an entirely different matter and becomes extremely difficult and complex to carry out.
What are the needs of the people? How many people do not have telephones? Why do they not have telephones? What is the proper rate of return that the company which provides the telephones should receive? All these are questions which the new agency will have to deal with. I suggest it is not enough to say that the agency will be given the responsibility of regulating telephone rates. We have to ask ourselves not just the policy questions which this government obviously has not even thought about- and which I have asked-but also if we have provided the old regulatory agency, the CTC, with the staff to really examine the costs of Bell Canada so that they can set a fair rate. We must also ask ourselves whether we will provide sufficient staff for the new regulatory agency, the expanded CRTC, to do the job. If one looks at the job which the CTC has done, whether it is on the question of railway freight rates, air rates, or telephones, it becomes obvious that the CTC has never had the necessary staff to really set, in any kind of realistic framework, the rates for any of these commodities or services.
We have been told that the number of employees the CTC has to work on telephone rates is not more than three people. I suggest that if that is true, it must be impossible for the CTC to do the job adequately and it will be just as impossible for the new CRTC. We want when this bill goes
Broadcasting
to committee, to be able to call witnesses representing consumer groups in order to find out what their experience has been when increases in telephone rates have been requested by Bell Telephone. We would like to call the CTC in order to find out whether it has had adequate staff in terms of numbers, experience and training and what kind of information it has been able to get from Bell Canada over the years; whether it has been able to get the information required in order to arrive at fair judgments as to what telephone rates should be each time an application for an increase has been made.
The CTC, in dealing with the last application for an increase, expressed the view that a rate adjustment formula should be adopted which would index the rates of Bell to various cost factors and therefore preclude hearings on rate increase requests from Bell which have been so frequent in recent years. The board seemed to feel that it wanted a formula which would guarantee the rate of profit for Bell. We oppose this kind of proposal and we would like to know whether the government endorsed this proposal of the Canadian Transport Commission.
If we are going to move toward the principle of a guaranteed annual income, we do not believe that the place to start is Bell Canada. Many people in this country-probably 25 per cent-are now living in a state of poverty, as calculated by the Economic Council or by the Senate committee which studied the question of poverty. I do not know whether the minister is still interested in the plight of ordinary people, but at the time of the asbestos workers' strike he showed a great deal of interest in the ordinary people. I hope he will continue to show this interest.
If we are to begin a guaranteed annual income program by guaranteeing the income of certain groups of people, let us begin with poor people and not with the shareholders of Bell Canada. In approving the last rate increase, the government said it would monitor the performance of Bell Canada, and that if Bell's profits exceeded an acceptable rate of return-which the government set at from 8.6 per cent to 9.1 per cent, which was itself up from an earlier 8.2 per cent and a maximum on a rate on economic equity of 12 per cent from an earlier 10.4 per cent-it would monitor the effect of the increases on the public.
When we get to committee, we in the NDP would like to know whether the government in fact has monitored Bell's performance since it permitted those increases. The minister nods his head to indicate that it has. The consumers of this country who have to deal with Bell Canada are not entirely satisfied with this government and with the mere nodding of the minister's head that it has monitored Bell. They would like to know the result of that monitoring. They would like to know how much profit Bell Canada has made in the last few years, because as sure as I am standing here today, Bell will be asking for another increase in the very near future.
I would be remiss in my duty if I did not take this opportunity to point out that the people of Ontario and Quebec will not have telephone service at fair and reasonable rates while Bell Canada remains a private company. Fair and reasonable rates cannot be achieved by monitor-

March 4, 1975
Broadcasting
ing; they can only be achieved for the people of Ontario and Quebec by bringing telephone systems under public ownership instead of allowing them to remain under private ownership as is the case with Bell Canada. I do not make this point in any spirit of doctrinaire narrowness. I do not make it necessarily because I believe in the theory of public ownership. I make it because the record in Canada shows that publicly-owned telephone systems provide competent and efficient service at lower rates than those charged by Bell Canada.
Long before the NDP existed as a political party, long before the CCF was a political party and long before any party espoused the principle of public ownership of basic services, the people of the three prairie provinces, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, enjoyed the benefits of publicly-owned telephone systems. In Manitoba, the publicly-owned telephone system was established some time between 1905 and 1910. It was established by the Conservative government headed by Sir Robert Roblin, the grandfather of the later Conservative premier, Duff Roblin. These publicly-owned systems are alive and well in the three prairie provinces. They provide modern and efficient service for the people of the provinces.
Let us do what the CTC consistently refuses to do, compare rates in the prairie provinces with rates in Ontario and Quebec. Let us compare the rates for villages, towns and cities. In every case we shall find that publicly-owned systems provide services at costs substantially below the costs of the services provided by Bell Canada in Ontario and Quebec. I shall put a few examples on record to let the minister know that what I am saying is correct. First, let us consider rates for exchanges governing between 2,000 and 5,000 stations. The residential rate, per month, at Drumheller, Alberta, is $3.65; at Melville, Saskatchewan, $3.36; at Thompson, Manitoba, $3.20; at Atiko-kan, Ontario, $4.46; and at Baie St.-Paul, Quebec, $4.59.
Let us consider rates in larger towns where exchanges govern between 10,000 and 20,000 stations. The rate at Clairmont, Alberta, is $4. That is the residential rate. The rate at Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan, is $3.89; at Brandon, Manitoba, $3.62; at Port Hope, Ontario, $5.04; and at Chapeau, Quebec, $5.18. These are all monthly rates. Let us consider towns over with 100,000 stations. The monthly rate in Calgary is $4.25; in Winnipeg, Manitoba, $4.10; in Burlington, Ontario, $6.09; and in Quebec City, $6.37.
The figures quoted speak for themselves and show what happens when telephone service is owned publicly or privately. If the minister is interested in the well-being of the people of his province and of Ontario, I suggest that he should consider the advisability of the government's taking over Bell Canada and operating it as a publicly-owned telephone system. This can, and should be done as a joint venture in which the two provinces concerned and the federal government participate. I have said we will support this bill and why we think it will serve to improve the regulation of telephone rates in Ontario and Quebec. I have mentioned our reservations. All the same, we have a good deal of confidence in the present members of the CTC. We are confident they will do the best job they can in regulating telephone rates. Having said that, I must repeat what I said previously, that telephone service will

be cheaper and better if it is provided by a publicly-owned
system.
Divisions of responsibility as between the federal government and the provinces have complicated the regulating of the various telecommunication services. We do not think the federal government should lay down policy unilaterally or establish agencies for regulating in this field without first consulting the provinces. Neither should it attempt unilaterally to police various fields of communication by establishing boards, agencies or other bodies the members of which are appointed entirely by the federal government. We think that the criticisms of all ten provinces are valid, that there should be a much greater exchange of ideas and that provincial requests for jurisdiction in this area to be fairly divided should be dealt with in a more co-operative fashion than has heretofore been evident. The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie will speak at greater length on this subject.
In committee we intend to question witnesses actively and aggressively. Many of our questions we hope, will be answered. Then when the bill returns to this House at a later stage, we shall know more than we do now about what the government intends to do.

As I said earlier, each province should have a representative in order to protect their own culture and education.

Mr. Speaker, on the occasion of a debate on such a bill, one can hardly resist the temptation of addressing this House, especially if one has the privilege of representing a Quebec constituency where people are always conscious of the various problems which concern the province of Quebec, as well as the Saint-Hyacinthe area.
The debate which opened this afternoon on Bill C-5 should be rather short considering the contents of the bill. At first glance, this looks like a harmless and perhaps trivial bill. Actually, this is a bill designed to create another commission made up of nine full-time members and ten part-time members and to set their salaries and fees. Such is essentially the purpose of this bill. It is obvious that the minister certainly intends to appoint as members of that commission, the most praiseworthy and qualified people, distinguished men and women who will really serve their country. He does not intend to use that new commission as a kind of haven for people who have well served the Liberal party.
Taking for granted the minister's good intentions that will be ascertained after the passage of the bill, it is very difficult to stay away from this debate. Besides the somewhat minor importance of the text before us, and therein lies the importance of this debate, this text has a scope, a meaning that must be analyzed and scrutinized, because we, from Quebec, are aware of the matters in dispute between the federal government and the Quebec government in respect of telecommunications and broadcasting.
A few days ago, the Quebec Minister of Communications had the opportunity to express in his own way on the CBC network, the views of his government and ask a few questions. The question is whether a government serves satisfactorily or not the people who elected it. The question is whether a government represents or not the interests of the people. It is a matter of knowing whether a government has the right to make certain claims, even though those claims are made to a federal government which, on occasion, feels almighty in certain jurisdictions.
I say then, Mr. Speaker, that this bill calls for detailed consideration on our part. I was delighted a while ago, to hear my colleague from Regina East (Mr. Balfour) with the his usual level-headedness, fully explain the point of view of the official opposition through observations that deserve the congratulations of all hon. members.
Mr. Speaker, during this debate, the minister will have the opportunity of answering the questions put to him publicly by the Quebec Minister of Communications last Sunday during a television program, namely: Sometime in April, will the minister agree to another meeting of the provincial ministers and the federal representative to discuss this contentious matter? This time, will there be more than palaver? Will negotiations really start? Will some importance really be given the claims of other provinces? Needless to say, Quebec is not the only party to this

quarrel: on the contrary. Quebec feels supported by several other provinces.
Those questions will be answered before the bill is read the econd time. Let me just say that consideration of this bill establishing the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission will give us the opportunity of finding out how the Canadian government feels about national unity. National unity has been talked about aimlessly at times and has been the subject of many speeches, but national unity should really be reflected in the actions of governments.
In the bill before us the government will have the opportunity of indicating very clearly what is its concept of national unity, how it wishes to further it and above all establish it across the country. If Canada was built, linked and united by the railways, as the eminent and congenial Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) said recently, paradoxically it is now divided on the matter of communications.
Since the Broadcasting Act of 1968 was adopted, no significant legislation has been enacted nor has any new commitment been undertaken, despite major technological changes and the justifiable concern of the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, we must hope and clamour, so as to make are sure to be heard, that the potential Commission provided for in Bill C-5 will first protect and ensure the development of political, social and economic life in Canada, second that it will contribute to ensure the movement and the exchange of regional and cultural information, and third, that it will also contribute to the development of national unity which is not factitious, which is not artificial, but which comes from a harmonization of our linguistic and cultural differences. It will also have to reflect the Canadian identity, the Canadian personality and the diversity of cultures and of social values in Canada. The Commission will also have to facilitate the orderly development of telecommunications in Canada by Canadians representing both founding groups of this country and to provide all Canadians with efficient and economical services and fair rates.
Mr. Speaker, in order to reach these objectives, the government will have to endeavor immediately to solve these problems with the intensive cooperation of the provinces. We could not emphasize too much this capital element of any policy which must be developed and defined by the central government.
We know quite well how important it is to respect the autonomy and rights of the provinces, to act towards them with much more flexibility, so that the conflicts that have been so frequent in recent history might be avoided. And it is precisely because this respect for provincial jurisdiction is almost an innate feeling that we say to the minister today that, if he wants to reach the aims I have just mentioned, there must be close cooperation with the provinces, not only for one or two days, at a seminar concluded by a press release which some parties are prepared to agree to while others refuse to do so. No!
There must be a continued and unceasing dialogue, an opening of mind towards the provinces, particularly towards Quebec, because the current conflicts between

broadcasting, teledistribution and transmission companies, on one hand, and those between provincial or federal jurisdictions on this matter, on the other hand, are such that they require from people in government much more flexibility than what we have been used to in the past.
Mr. Speaker, it is completely abnormal that, on communications, as the headlines I have mentioned earlier can show, Quebec and Ottawa should not see eye to eye. It is paradoxical. Therefore the federal Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier) must suggest administrative arrangements to the provinces and guarantee them real participation in national regulatory agencies. Furthermore, he must establish with the provinces the respective jurisdictions of the federal and provincial governments on this matter.
The CRTC maintains that the federal government has exclusive jurisdiction over broadcasting and cablevision. But there are other people, such as legal expert Gordon Henderson of Ottawa, who believe that the existing Broadcasting Act does not bear a clear mention of the federal jurisdiction on cablevision.
As you are all aware, the position of Quebec minister L'Allier on cablevision has already been supported by Ontario, Manitoba and Alberta, and whatever the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Duclos) who interrupted me a while ago might think, Ontario and Manitoba do not to my knowledge have separatist governments and the ministers of communications in those provinces, who support the claims of the Quebec minister, do not have separatist tendencies and are not about to leave confederation.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think that in these circumstances, we must expose the situation vigorously. And I hope that I shall not be the only one to do so, and that other Quebec members on both sides of the House will join me in exposing very clearly, objectively and responsibly the rigidity of the federal government, and in strongly urging the federal Minister of Communications to negotiate with his provincial counterparts without always holding up the ultimate weapon of the Supreme Court. There will always be an opportunity to do so.
It should be noted, Mr. Speaker, that in such cases the solution is not always for the courts to decide. When such differences have political implications, the responsibility lies with political authorities to arrive at permanent solutions through dialogue, talks and meetings, instead of shifting the burden on the courts in the hope that their decision will put an end to litigations or wrangles.
As far as Quebec is concerned in this matter, the federal Minister of Communications should not ponder, as the Prime Minister did, whether that province's government is popular or not when it makes claims of a rather embarrassing nature. It will be quite enough for the minister to realize, for instance, that at the bottom of that difference lies a basic concern of Quebecers who want to have a say on technological developments in communications. This Quebec wish that I am expressing in this House contains or hides no cultural sovereignty trap. It is amazing, Mr. Speaker, how some politicians are in fear of being trapped by words. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I see it is only five minutes before the private members' hour so I will not have that much time to get into detail on Bill C-5 presently before the House.
This bill is an attempt by the government to combine the existing Canadian Transport Commission and the Canadian Radio-television Commission into one super agency to deal with the growing problems in respect of communications in this country. Because we have such a technological explosion in terms of communications we find that legislation designed many years ago, as early as the time of Confederation, is inadequate to meet the needs of communications in this very complex world.
Many scientists are predicting what they call "the wire city" with the advent of the coaxial cable which is now bringing television to many households in the country. They foresee the time when this same cable can be used to transmit other forms of computer messages, whereby someone can do his shopping by means of a telephone hook-up. I believe there is already an experiment being conducted in Toronto whereby a person can dial directly to a department store catalogue computer service, and order items in that fashion.
As a result of this expansion in cable service we are getting into jurisdictional disputes. Under the constitution the federal government was to be in charge of broadcasting, and at the time this meant mainly telegraph service.

Then we moved into broadcasting by means of airways. With the advent of cable there are additional jurisdictional disputes because the provinces, through their telephone companies, claim the right to regulate cable service.
We are now faced with a question as to the definition of broadcasting; does it include cable television and, if so, who has jurisdiction, the federal government or the provinces? This bill is an attempt to deal with these very complex problems. They are complex, indeed, because in spite of the attempts of the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier) to sit down with the provinces and come up with some kind of agreement, there has been very little success to date.
During my speech I should like to analyze what I think are some of the pitfalls in attempting to set up this super regulatory agency, and outline what I think will be some of the weaknesses. I want also to offer some suggestions to the minister on how he can improve communications with the provincial governments in order to resolve this very complex problem of jurisdiction.
I see it is five o'clock. Mr. Speaker, may I call it five o'clock and continue at eight this evening?

speechtext: The House res'umed consideration of the motion of Mr. Pelletier (Hochelaga) that Bill C-5, to establish the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission, to amend the Broadcasting Act and other acts in consequence thereof and to enact other consequential provisions, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts.

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to resume my comments on Bill C-5, on which I began to speak prior to the adjournment at five o'clock for private members' hour.
This bill was brought forward by the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier) to combine the existing regulatory bodies, the Canadian Transport Commission and the Canadian Radio-television Commission, into one super regulatory agency. I said earlier this afternoon that we in the NDP have some major criticisms about this proposal. Our first reservation is that the history of super regulatory agencies-such as the parallel agency in the United States which is the Federal Communications Commission-shows that the large agency tends to be subservient to the communications corporation interest. In fact what happens is that they tend to allow vertical integration and the strengthening of the monopoly of a few key industries in the communications system.
We also find, judging from the American example, that such huge regulatory bodies of common carriers develop a fixation on technology. In other words, the medium rather than the message becomes the most important thing. The body becomes concerned about regulating the actual hardware of cable television, wave television, and other aspects of the communication system, and looks at the technology rather than the content. It seems to us very important that this super agency should not diminish its role in examining the medium, the content of television, radio, telecommunication and other related areas.
My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), pointed out earlier this afternoon the lamentable record of the Canadian Transport Commission in standing up for citizens' interests against corporation interests. I do not want to go into that in too much detail, but suffice it to say that example after example has shown that when CPR or Bell Canada came before the CTC asking for a rate increase, usually they got it, and consumer groups attempting to put forward their case were hindered by lack of resources and lack of funds. They could not match the phalanx of lawyers or experts that the big corporations had to present their cases before the CTC.
Our hope is that because the CTC has such a lamentable record, the new super agency will correct some of that imbalance whereby the CTC has tended to listen more intently to the presentations of the large corporations rather than to individuals or consumer groups.
[The Acting Speaker (Mrs. Morin).]
The CRTC has had a somewhat better record regarding regulating broadcasting, promoting Canadian content and trying to regulate advertising. I am not saying that the record of CRTC is perfect, but certainly to make a comparison between its concern and that of the CTC about content and Canadian identity, and perhaps to some degree consumerism, its record is much more laudable than that of the CTC.
We hope that in the new agency the philosophy and approach of the CRTC will prevail rather than that of the CTC. However, somehow I have doubts about that because no matter what agency one sets up unless there is a strong minister, and a government setting out clear guidelines and making sure its agency pursues those guidelines in a vigorous way, it is doomed to failure in protecting the public's interest.
There are two questions that really need to be answered about the new agency proposed in Bill C-5. The first is, how strong will be the guidelines which the government will give to the agency? The second is, how adequate will its backup staff be to supervise those guidelines? Turning first to the guidelines, we notice already that one of the major weaknesses of the CTC is that the government has not ensured that the CTC vigorously pursued some of the guidelines set by the original legislation.
The Canadian Transport Commission was set up in light of the fact that we have monopoly institutions in this country in transportation and communications. The CTC was designed to protect the public interest. We know that the government and its predecessors have been somewhat lax in seeing that that goal was upheld. For instance, in the minority twenty-ninth parliament when the New Democratic Party was able to bring some pressure to bear on behalf of Canadian consumers, we prevented a further increase in Bell Telephone rates by arguing that in light of the profit position of Bell the increase was unjustified. Now that we have a majority parliament we see that decision reversed, and the government allowing the rate increase.
What I am saying is that we must have clear guidelines for the new regulatory agency, and we must have a government which will stand up and force the agency to pursue those guidelines vigorously.
The CRTC, despite its somewhat better record than that of the CTC, also has a number of weaknesses. Again it is a problem of the government not backing the agency or giving it the power to pursue its original mandate in a very vigorous way. I quote from the mandate given to the CRTC. This is in the Broadcasting Act, section 3(g). It states that the national broadcasting service should, and I quote:
be a balanced service of information, enlightenment and entertainment for people of different ages, interests and tastes covering the whole range of programming in fair proportion.
And from the same act:
-contribute to the development of national unity and provide for a continuing expression of Canadian identity.
Those are laudable aims and guidelines for the CRTC, and yet when we look at the past policy decisions of this regulatory agency we find that it has fallen somewhat
March 4, 1975

short of those intentions. I give as an example the recent licensing of a new English television network in Canada, the Global television network. This was done without prior policy hearings throughout the country. Here we have a situation where a third television network is set up in Canada, although the Global network is basically just in southern and central Ontario despite the fact that if a third network is justified, we really need one based more in western Canada.
One of the great criticisms of the CBC and the CTV is that they are located in central Canada, and they express that kind of viewpoint. Many of their stories and personnel originate from that area of the country, and western Canadians, I think quite justifiably, feel that only the central part of Canada is getting attention. News comes with a particular bias from that region, and the west does not have a voice. It must be irksome to people in western Canada to hear Toronto oriented news stories, just as much as it is for us in northern Ontario. Here is an example of the CRTC not really carrying through its mandate to have full hearings on the establishment of a third television network.
I have a criticism of the CRTC on its lack of success in diverting cablevision revenue into general broadcasting, and also its failure to promote non commercial television service. I think there is a place in Canada for a non commercial service. I think this is what the CBC should be. We know that the CBC radio network is moving in that direction, and I think it would be a good test to allow the CBC television also to move toward a non commercial status. Then we could compare the private networks with a non commercial national network. The CRTC has not really pressed for this development, and I think that is quite lamentable.
My third criticism of the CRTC-and again I am using this as an illustration to point out that unless the government sets clear guidelines and gives the agency the power to pursue them, we have an agency in name rather than in fact-is that the CRTC has the power to make regulations regarding broadcasting, but its great drawback is that it cannot deal with the financial implications of such decisions. For example, the CRTC recently moved to reduce commercials on CBC television, especially children's commercials.
The interesting thing is that when the CRTC passes an edict down to the CBC saying that it must remove or reduce children's commercials, the CRTC has no power to authorize introduction of estimates in this parliament to make up for the loss of revenue suffered by the CBC television network. The CRTC then cannot provide funding for such reforms, and therefore its hands are tied. I fear that the new regulatory agency will be in the same boat.
Another example is that the CRTC is quite strong on Canadian content, as it should be. We have moved toward higher Canadian content in radio, but I give the example of the CRTC demanding 60 per cent Canadian content for the CTV network and then having to back down because CTV said it could not possibly manage it, and a compromise of only 50 per cent Canadian content was reached in return for extended service. In other words, because the CRTC is forced to allow television to solicit advertising
Broadcasting
revenue-and I find it almost incredible that with a publicly owned national network we have 12 minutes of advertising per hour on television, which is more than the private American networks-we have this conflict of interest where the CRTC is supposed to regulate advertising, but at the same time recognizes that it cannot do very much against advertising because of its inability to provide alternate funding or to recommend with any force alternate funding for these television networks.
I find it very sad that the CRTC has refused to act on a growing problem facing television in this country, and that is the use of advertising. I am afraid that in certain circumstances advertising has now taken on the air of political propaganda. I give as an example the recent series of commercials by Imperial Oil on Hockey Night in Canada, where this foreign owned company is making a political statement about the necessity of having higher revenues, by implication saying that the governments are taking too much in taxes and have created a supply crisis in this country. There is no provision for advertisements to counter that kind of political propaganda, and either the CRTC should demand that these commercials stop or at least provide an alternative opportunity for rebuttal, which it has not been doing. I think that that is a very serious indication of what is happening to advertising when large, multinational corporations can twist the intent of the Broadcasting Act and be allowed to put this kind of commercial on the national network without any chance of correction or rebuttal.
What I am saying is that if we are going to have this new super agency, we must have strength and guidelines. We cannot have a repetition of the kind of activity where the CTC favours large corporations over the private consumer. Nor should the CRTC be further weakened by unclear guidelines. The agency must be given power to implement its mandate. Adequate guidelines are essential for the work of a regulatory agency. I doubt if the government is serious about implementing such guidelines.
The second question I raise is, how adequate will be the staffing of the new regulatory agency? Obviously, if you combine under one agency two former agencies, you will double the workload of the new agency. According to the bill, serving on this agency will, be nine full-time and ten part-time directors. Compare that with the present board of the CRTC. Today there are five full-time and ten part-time directors serving on that body. Clearly the workload of the new agency will be increased and fewer directors will handle it; therefore the directors will be overworked.
Equally important is the size of the office support staff. Because the field of communications is complex, it must be studied. Many briefs will have to be read, analysed and processed. Large businesses dealing with the new agency can hire dozens of lawyers and technical experts to present briefs which, in effect, overwhelm agency staff. Unless the support staff is enlarged, the proposed agency will find itself in the same predicament as the CTC and, to a lesser extent, the CRTC.
When a regulatory body receives hundreds of pages of briefs and dozens of volumes of data from a company like
