Bell, can you imagine how hard it is to examine such material? If regulatory bodies find this task hard, can you imagine how hard it is for consumer groups which lack the staff of an agency and the expertise available to businesses appearing before it?
Who will be on the board of this super regulatory agency? Will it be staffed only by lawyers, engineers and technocrats? If so, the new agency will act in the same way as the FCC in the United States has acted. The technocrats on the American commission are more concerned about the medium than the message. Such a step in this country would be a backward one. If broadcasters are included on the board of directors, how can we avoid conflicts of interest? Perhaps these questions can best be answered in committee.
The bill has not provided for any consumer advisory bureau which would assist consumers to prepare briefs or oppose communication oriented companies seeking to increase rates. Such a bureau should be established to assist consumers, and to help them travel from various parts of Canada to attend hearings here in Ottawa. Consumers found it difficult to travel from various parts of the country to Ottawa to attend CRTC and CTC hearings. The average consumer or consumer group cannot compete successfully with experts available to corporations. If the minister is serious about establishing an agency which will hear both sides of the story, he must amend the bill and provide for the establishment of a consumer bureau that will provide technical and expert advice, and funds as well, to enable consumers to travel, hire lawyers, and present their case before the board. We of the NDP hope the new agency will not repeat the mistakes of existing agencies. We hope it will move in a new direction and protect the public interest.
This bill sets the stage for the first battle between the provinces and the federal government over which will regulate broadcasting and cable television in this country. Broadcasting is now more complex than ever and cannot be equated merely with the transmission of waves through the air. Signals are transmitted via coaxial cable, the implications of which are immense. People will be able to hook into a computer circuit directly and order a product, pay a bill, or obtain information. What has been called the "wired city" is growing and will affect future developments in this country. Therefore it is important that we establish ground rules as to who will control what.
The federal and provincial governments are arguing over jurisdiction. Traditionally the federal government has controlled the airwaves and, hence, broadcasting. Traditionally the provinces have controlled telephone service and therefore claim jurisdiction over cable, which will be used in future for broadcasting and computer retrieval systems.
It is worth reviewing the positions of the provinces to help us keep the provisions of this bill in perspective. At the federal communications conference Alberta suggested that the provincial government "must have an input into the regulation of cable." Alberta officials stated that if its benefits are to be brought to their scattered people outside the densely populated urban areas, there must be a provincial master plan. This means an involvement of the provinces in the setting of franchise boundaries and the regu-
lation of rates. Provinces are legitimately concerned about the nature of cable television within provincial jurisdictions.
Ontario stated that because of the local nature of cable television the government of Ontario believes it must be responsible for the franchise area, the granting of the franchise and the designation of the services to be supplied, including educational, community and household services, and all-closed circuit aspects such as pay TV and information retrieval.
The position of Saskatchewan was that national broadcasting policy must balance the need to support the development of a viable production industry against the need to extend broadcasting distribution to all Canadians. Saskatchewan too is concerned about developing this network to serve remote communities of the province.
The position of Manitoba was that decentralization of control of cable television was a means of reversing the rural-urban shift. The potential for regional development which could result from a realistic decentralization of federal government electronic data processing activities was promising.
What was the attitude of the government of Quebec? I am worried, because so far no Quebec Liberal members have spoken in this debate. The attitude of the Premier of Quebec is important. He said, and I quote:
In cultural matters, the decision making centres we require for our own cultural security must be transferred, especially in the field of communications. This again is a simple matter of common sense since an English-speaking majority cannot be entrusted with ensuring the cultural security of a French-speaking minority. My government's position on this matter could be flexible as to form, but as far as the basic issues and the objectives are concerned, it is, and will remain firm, clear and determined.
Here we see the concern of the premier of Quebec about provincial jurisdiction in order to protect the cultural indentity of the French language group.
British Columbia is also concerned about jurisdiction over cable. Its officials say that an effective national policy in communications must respect the diversity of regions by being sufficiently flexible to permit varying solutions to diverse communications problems. A flexible national policy must accommodate the exercise of federal and provincial responsibilities in the implementation of differing policies among regions.
That, in brief form, is a summary of the attitudes of some of the provinces. The key theme running through this is that the provinces want to have an input into communications policy. They have certain regional and educational priorities for their people. They have a desire to protect their cultural identity and develop a regional consciousness. As a result, they need to have a say in communications policy making.
Against that we have the position of the federal government that says it has to govern for all of Canada. It says it has to promote a sense of Canadian identity and unity.
The federal government was somewhat taken aback by the united front of provinces wanting control over cable television as I have outlined. We are now faced with a problem which this bill just begins to touch on, the prob-
March 4, 1975

lem of jurisdiction over cable. How can we reconcile the legitimate needs of the provinces to service their residents against the legitimate need of the federal government to promote national unity rather than allow the country to be balkanized by all kinds of independent provincial communications systems?
There is a choice for the federal government and the provinces. They can go one of two ways. They can take the legal route and try to settle this conflict by taking the matter to the Supreme Court. If they do that, the provinces must recognize that the decision will have to come down in favour of the federal government. I say this because of the decision given in 1932 by the Privy Council which gave the federal government complete jurisdiction over regulation and control of radio communications. The Supreme Court is bound to favour the federal government in any legal battle over who has ultimate authority and control. However, I do not think the Minister of Communications wants to take that route. He knows it would be divisive. It would cause much hard feeling and division within the country, and hinder the ultimate aim of national unity and a sense of Canadian identity.
The other, and perhaps the only choice open, is the consultative route. This route would serve the best interests of national unity. It is a route that the provinces and the federal government must follow. I regret to say that so far there has been very little progress in this area. It is obvious that we need provincial input into this new super regulatory agency. Mechanisms must be established in order to allow the provinces to argue their case before the federal government, stating why they need special development of cable communications, radio or educational television within their provincial jurisdiction.
I was interested in a letter which the Minister of Communications sent to the Hon. John Rhodes, Ontario minister of transport and communications. The letter is dated September 18, 1974. The Minister of Communications proposed four points as a means of taking this consultative route. First is the establishment of a continuing committee on communications policy, comprising the responsible federal and provincial ministers. Second is the establishment of an association of federal and provincial regulatory commissions dealing with communications. Third is provincial approval of part-time members nominated to serve on the federal regulatory body, a body which this bill will create. Fourth is participation by representatives of provincial regulatory bodies in deliberations of the federal regulatory body.
Those proposals seem sound. It is a constructive route that the provinces and the federal government can follow, yet we see very little of any such proposals coming to fruition. Indeed in Bill C-5 there is a glaring absence of any reference to the third proposal of the minister, namely, allowing the provinces to approve part-time members nominated to serve on the federal regulatory body.
One wonders what kind of communication, if any, is going on between the federal minister and his provincial counterparts. What I have heard to date leads me to believe there is very little constructive consultation going on. There is not a meeting of minds. The lines are beginning to harden; positions are becoming more rigid.
Broadcasting
I hope we do not get backed into a corner and have to face a legal constitutional battle over this issue of jurisdiction in the field of communications. As reasonable Canadians concerned not only with provincial but national rights, I hope that the federal minister and the provincial communications ministers will put less importance on who has the final say regarding the medium, and be more concerned about working out ways to have input into the message carried by this medium. In the end that is what is most important. If we do not have a content that is Canadian, alive and vigorous, promoting a Canadian identity as well as serving regional needs, we will have failed in a vital area of this country's future growth. We need to have a sound communications system.
Perhaps a compromise could be that the provinces would licence cable television to conform to the new CRTC guidelines. Perhaps it might be possible for a certain percentage of television time to be made available for provincial input. There are many areas which could be explored in a true spirit of co-operation between the central government and the provinces and, heaven knows, we certainly need more co-operation than confrontation. I hope the new regulatory agency will not repeat the mistakes made by the CTC and CRTC but that it will move in a new direction.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take advantage of the debate on the bill before us in order to comment briefly, perhaps too briefly, on matters which I feel should be dealt with but which, for one reason or another, have so far been avoided in the course of our discussion. Before I get to what I consider to be the main substance of what I have to say I should like to deal generally with the broadcasting and television of programs in Canada.
The act as it presently stands makes provision for identifying Canadians to other Canadians. However, in the implementation of the relevant sections it would appear that because of the concentration of population in certain areas of the country and the impact these powerful groupings have on the executive, and, possibly on the bureaucracy, to say nothing of the government and its supporters, the regulations have either been ignored or else have been very laxly interpreted. As a result, many parts of the country are still without broadcasting facilities. Many briefs have been presented on their behalf to one body or another in an attempt to redress this situation, but for reasons of economy, it is said, the eyes of the CBC, the government and the commission have always been focussed on the larger centres of population.
However, I believe the point has now been reached at which far greater emphasis should be placed on serving the more sparsely populated regions of Canada. The people living there are making a contribution to our way of life and they naturally wish to enjoy other aspects of the Canadian scene, brought into their own livingrooms as in the case of other Canadians. At the present time they seem to be treated as second rate citizens in this respect.

March 4, 1975
Broadcasting
Hon. members have referred to the rights of provincial authorities and have noted how jealously the provinces guard those rights. Let us think in terms of still smaller groups of population, of minorities; one can imagine the frustration they feel when their representations are ignored year after year simply because they do not reflect the views of great numbers of people. I feel that when the government is drawing up regulations as guidelines in consultation with the commission it should recognize the situation, and ensure that when licences for broadcasting or televising are issued, those directly concerned are made fully aware of their responsibilities to provide services of the kind I have in mind.
For example, there are many native groups, particularly in northern areas such as I represent, who are desirous of making a contribution and would like broadcasting to be done in their language. I might say that CBC radio has done an admirable job in this field. Radios are carried around in these sparsely populated areas, along trap lines and so on. Trappers, prospectors and others who live in the north use radios to pick up messages as well as for entertainment; they are one of the few contacts they have with the outside world. We have an obligation to these Canadians and, in my opinion, more emphasis should be placed on serving their needs rather than continuing in the fashion we have developed. Those who live in or near urban areas already have a wide selection of programs available to them.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the private companies have managed to take care of the financial problem surrounding the introduction of coloured television. For years it was argued that funds were insufficient to extend broadcasting to remote areas. However, when it came to opening up the country to coloured television, described at the time as being an extremely expensive process, funds came from somewhere. They were found because densely populated areas were able to exert a greater impact upon the government or upon the members of the commission. There is strength in numbers.
I wish to deal now with another area which should be covered because I feel a sense of frustration as a member of parliament. I feel the old Broadcasting Act, the original set-up of the CRTC, has had ample time to test out certain areas as to which way they should go. There are many members of the House of Commons who would like to comment on what I wish to say, but who feel a sense of frustration because they want to be lenient and allow the operation of our broadcasting system in such a way that censorship should not have to be exercised.
I think the intent of many members who participated in the original discussions on the act, in the committee or in the House, was that in no way should there be censorship. But what we expected from the commission was common sense. What we did not want was to see some little group allowing itself all the power and becoming untouchable in the sense that if you tamper with them you are immediately accused of censoring them. If you comment, you are a prude, you are not "with it," you are a "has-been," you are not an intellectual.
Surely every parent who cares how he brings up his family has the task of showing his offspring the difference between right and wrong. We enact regulations. We set up

green lights and red lights. We set up rules everywhere in society. Yet we give television producers in many cases absolute licence to pull the rug out from every service club, every church, every mother and father who gives a darn about their children because they want to show us that they can produce something that defies everyone and get away with it.
I am as concerned about the use of censorship as anybody. I am proud to be in a country where we can express ourselves freely. But I hate to be identified as one of a small minority. I had a very complimentary article written about me and I know I am living in the real world, but I do not think it is necessary to exploit sex on television or to use vulgar language. It is not that I am self-righteous, but I do want to speak for all those who cannot speak for themselves on this question. The message must get through to those who are charged with responsibility for our broadcasting system.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) once said that the state has no business in the bedrooms of the nation. I say that I do not want to see sex as the symbol of our society. I realize the commission has a heavy role to fulfil, but as members of parliament have an obligation to society, so does the CRTC.
There seems to be a headlong rush to use advertising in order to get the greatest impact. Much use is made of television's instant message which reaches millions of people. However, by allowing certain freedoms people are able to corrupt. A few people will not be corrupted whatever the effort, but the constant use of corruption on television and certain filthy programs on television tend to undermine society. It is like an apple that is rotting from within. If this is what we expect society to be, Mr. Speaker, then I and all the people who write me are wrong.
I think the regulations as originally written were designed to steer a very fine course between censorship and freedom of expression. I have had people ask me, if a certain program was obscene, why those responsible have not been charged. But why should I or some other individual have to go to the trouble of charging these people simply because they took it upon themselves to produce something that breeds corruption? Why should we expect this of Canadian citizens? Surely there are other means of getting the message across.
This commission will be a body comprising nine full time members and ten part time members. I often wonder what happens to certain categories of submissions and whether they are automatically turned down. I have seen some of the submissions made to the commission, as I am sure other hon. members have, and I do not think that the people I represent are any different from the constituents of other hon. members. If the minister does not have sufficient authority to control the CRTC, then perhaps we should give him that authority, but these people have it in their power to cleanse themselves. Common logic should tell them what is right and what is wrong. This is not the case with the CBC television.

The untouchables.
March 4, 1975

subtopic: COMMCHS DEBATES
speechtext:
Yes, the untouchables. If it is the will of parliament to allow the CBC this kind of freedom, then at least I should have the option to withhold some portion of the money that goes towards the upkeep of a machine that corrupts society.
I realize that some people will point out that if I do not like certain programs I can always switch them off. But I do not think that a subject like sex should be exploited before millions of people. If we do not view certain programs there is naturally a certain curiosity among young people as to why this is so. I do not think a few people in the television broadcasting industry should put us in that position. Neither do I think people should have to write to me and tell me there is something wrong, and ask me what I can do about it. I am sure that every member of this House has received letters of complaint; certainly most hon. members have.

subtopic: COMMCHS DEBATES
speechtext: I have.

subtopic: COMMCHS DEBATES
speechtext:
And so, Mr. Speaker, what are we going to do about this? I do not think we should be called upon as members, each and everyone, to stand in our place and announce that we have received complaints of this sort; I think there are sufficient complaints to date to place the facts before the minister and the commission. Surely they must be aware of these complaints by now. However, they tend to play it cool, and after a little while they again test us to see how far they can go. For my money they have gone too far.
Are the full and part time members of the commission going to take upon themselves the responsibility of taking action, or does parliament have to ask them to travel across the country at the expense of the public to find out for themselves? That should not be necessary. If there is a group in Canada whose submissions will not be heard, then I say we should scrap the whole commission, start again from square one, and see whether or not we can appoint members of the commission who do at least take heed of the concerns of society.
I hear so many people say these days that we have a permissive society. What has made it permissive? I suggest that what has made it permissive is nothing else but the repetition of this kind of program we see on television. When things are repeated often enough people begin to believe they are true. Here I can think of a word that has now become commonly used in the King's English but which was not known prior to the last war, and that word is blitzkrieg.
This type of permissiveness has become common on CBC radio and television, although perhaps I should separate the two because I think radio has done an admirable job. These people in television know they have a great impact on society, and they continue to corrupt our people. I suggest they know what they are doing. I do not consider them stupid, but they think that everyone else in society is stupid.
If the committee is to be charged with the responsibility of drawing up certain guidelines for the communications media I suggest the committee should do just that, because it is high time we had some guidelines. The regulations up
Broadcasting
to now have been faulty or inadequate. Obviously there are too many people who are willing to ignore them with this permissive type of programming.
Perhaps someone in the television media has already been charged under a section of the Criminal Code dealing with obscenity, but I am not aware of such a case. Perhaps this has not happened because the Criminal Code is not precise enough in those sections that deal with broadcasting. They deal adequately with writings and pictures but they do not deal specifically with television programs. Perhaps if there is an obligation on us we should accept it and change the Criminal Code in this respect. If the Broadcasting Act fails in this regard we should rewrite it, and perhaps the time to do it is during the committee hearings on this bill.
It is not good enough for us just to live with the situation or ignore it in the hope that it will go away, or just wait until we see what happens. I think we have had ample opportunity to see what has happened. I do not want to have to stand here again in the House of Commons, or have someone else make a speech on behalf of those people who are right in suggesting that certain programs are smutty. There are times when one defends a minority even though it might be wrong because one thinks perhaps it might do some good. In that case one does not mind being associated with such a group. However, in the case of the broadcasting media, particularly television, our regulations are wrong, or at least inadequate.
It has been often suggested that there is something wrong with our society because of the amount of crime and the increase in the rate of crime. We spend all kinds of money on treatment in our jails and rehabilitation centres. Very often when young people find themselves in jail we hear people making the excuse that society is at fault. They suggest that because a young offender comes from a poor family out in the sticks he has never had a chance in life. What kind of a chance are we giving our young people when we allow this type of permissiveness on CBC? Just because one or two individuals in the CBC say this is right, that does not make it so. When these people make such a decision we instantaneously get their message.
I began my remarks by saying I would be brief. Perhaps I have not spoken long enough yet to impress upon members the message I want to leave. I suggest we must look into this matter very seriously. I know the country wants us to do that. I know the people want us to do something about this type of smutty programming. The time to do something is right now, and the place is here. I suggest the minister would endear himself to a great many people in this country if he would take the step which will lead to a change in this situation, and the best feature of all is that by doing so he would be doing the right thing.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although I do not have many friends here, those I have are real
friends.
The Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier) introduced a bill to establish the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission, to amend the

March 4, 1975
Broadcasting
Broadcasting Act and other acts and to enact other consequential provisions.
My remarks will be very brief, but very specific. Since everyone knows the procedure in this House, whereby each bill goes through five stages before being finally either carried, killed or amended-in other words first reading, second reading and referral to Standing committee, the report stage and, finally, third reading. After that, the other place approves what we did. I therefore feel I will have other opportunities to deal with this bill's aims and objectives, and I wish to restrict my remarks to two clauses of the bill, more specifically clause 7(1) and (2), and clause 11(c). In the meantime, we will come back to clause 10 stating the number of meetings.
Mr. Speaker, it will be apparent why I deal so specifically with this bill, ever since I came to this House, in 1968. Bills are constantly introduced by Government members to establish Commissions, Committees, structures of some kind or Crown corporations. Each time a new bureaucracy is set up. Each time, it gets almost unlimited powers. It may not be in the act, but it happens in fact. Take the Unemployment Insurance Commission for instance. That commission has an advisory committee. Yet the act is specific in that case but God knows what they do. Neither you nor I, Mr. Speaker, can determine what kind of work they do, how much they are paid to do it, what are the results, since they are not accountable to Parliament.
Now, the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier), in an area and a field of operation, as important as communications are in a modern world, introduced a bill to create another "creature" of civil servants, another board. That one will be the Radio-television Commission.
Mr. Speaker, I see the former President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) who, when he was in that portfolio, was tightening the purse strings saying: Let us not spend too much. Mr. Speaker, when this House, on December 19 last, gave a first class burial to Bill C-44 to increase the salaries of members of parliament, the Public Service Alliance was protesting on the CBC and English and French television stations. The President of the public servants union, of those "creatures", said that members of parliament were paid too much, that it was disgusting, that enough was enough, that members of parliament were setting a bad example with their salary increase, and that those salaries were exaggerated. That is what I heard on the air that the Minister wants to control where the President of the union representing the public servants of those "creatures" expressed his views.
Mr. Speaker, tonight the House is considering a bill to create a "creature". That does not mean it will not serve the interests of the Canadians and this House. That means that it will provide jobs for Canadians, and it will become another superstructure of civil servants. How much will they be paid? How many times a year will they meet? What will be the respective and specific terms of reference of every member? There will be nine full-time and ten part-time, for a total of 19, as provided in the act.
Let us try and see, Mr. Speaker. Those very people who passed judgment on members of parliament, protected in

doing so by certain governments and NDP members, had this to say at clause 7(1):
Each full-time member shall be paid a salary to be fixed by the Governor in Council-
What is the salary, Mr. Speaker? I ask the minister through you. What will the salary be?
... and each part-time member shall be paid such fees for attendances at meetings of the Commission or any committee thereof or at any public hearing before the Commission that he is requested by the Chairman to attend as are fixed by by-law of the Commission.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the catch. Friends of the government will probably be appointed, as a political reward, to the Commission, and they will provide for their salaries and expense accounts through internal economy. Newspapermen will know nothing about that. They do not attend those meetings of the Commission. Nor do hon. members. No one will be able to judge them because they will be answerable to no one but a silent minister in this House who will tell us, as in the case of the CBC: Listen, the CBC is answerable to me, but this information is privileged. Mr. Speaker, those people will get paid, believe you me! But when the hon. members ask for a salary increase, people judge them, ask them to account for themselves: yet, the salaries paid those people come from the same source as those of the members of parliament.
Paragraph (2), Mr. Speaker, and I know this will be of interest to my colleague from Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) of the New Democratic Party: he understands those things; he is here to defend the interests of our fellow-citizens rather than those of the civil servants. I am sure of that. He agrees with me.
Paragraph (2) says this:
Each member is entitled to be paid such ... expenses ...
He is ordered to do so by law, Mr. Speaker, which is not the case for the people's elected representatives.
Subclause 7(2) of this bill stipulates that:
... be paid such travelling and living expenses incurred by him in the performance of his duties as are fixed by by-law of the Commission.
It would be fantastic, Mr. Speaker, if we could also operate by by-law, whatever the Canadian people may think, building an empire of civil servants, such as unemployment insurance offices, the Polymer Corporation, the CBC, which are answerable to nobody in this House nor to the general public.
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to put these remarks on record so that the same people who read in Hansard about the outcry against the salaries of MPs can see what is being done in this House about the establishment of a Radio-television Commission.
The minister who wanted to make sure that these people would be well paid before beginning to work indcluded two clauses to that effect, clauses 7 and 11. Surely he is not responsible for that, because in that case as in others, civil servants stick together.
Clause 11, subclause (c), in fact the first three pages of this bill, Mr. Speaker, do not deal with broadcasting protection and Canadian cable T.V. In fact, these are only dealt with in the schedule. The first six pages of this bill, Mr. Speaker, do not deal with the interests of Canadian people, nor with the use of airwaves, nor with private
March 4, 1975

interests or the bereavement of monopolies, nor even with the protection of Canadian interests with respect to the benefit foreign countries might derive from airwave use. In fact, the first six or seven pages of this bill aim at making sure that the civil servants employed will be well paid, well fed, will sleep well and have adequate transportation, and that everything will be handsomely provided for by the state's treasury. The broad objects of those people are outlined in the schedule.
Madam Speaker, this is how clause 11, subclause (c) reads:
11. The Commission may make by-laws ...
(c) fixing the fees to be paid to part-time members of the Commission for attendance at meetings of the Commission or any committee
thereof or at public hearings ...
Madam Speaker, we are in the process of establishing a special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons to study the immigration policy after the green paper on immigration. Members of Parliament will travel throughout the country doing exactly the same job as those civil servants besides listening to citizens, which civil servants don't. And those hon. members will not be paid for the work, but they will do exactly the same thing. They will carry out additional activities, but they will not get any complementary salary. Their expenses will not be paid, and on the contrary, everything will be at their own expense.
Madam Speaker, a bill is being introduced today. The members of the commission have not yet started to work, but they are assured that they will be paid at a rate determined not by the minister, not by the representatives of the people, not by Parliament either, but by themselves: that is what appears under "by-laws" in clause 11, subclause (c).
How many times will they meet every year? Members of Parliament meet I do not know how many hours and days every year. It is 9.15 p.m. just now, and none of us will receive any overtime pay because the House will adjourn around 10.30 p.m. The same thing happens three times a week. So, these people are going to meet, as provided under clause 10. Well, that remains to be seen, Madam Speaker, it is our duty to study legislation. Clause 10 reads as follows:
10. (2) The Commission shall meet at least six times in each year.
What a big success!
It is a real shame, Madam Speaker. I want the minister to know that before dealing with broadcasting, we should have a policy of equity between members of parliament and those who are merely appointed to administer the statutes passed by Parliament.
I feel that if we wanted to be logical in this House, we should see to it that the same rules, self-discipline, regulations and obligations that apply to us also apply to those civil servants who make fun of us when we vote ourselves salary increases. Then, we could listen to what they have to say.
Madam Speaker, my greatest source of frustration as a member is to have someone dictate to me some regulations about which I have no say and which are meant to be complementary to the legislation which I passed in the House. We pass the legislation, the officials make the
Broadcasting
regulations and finally we no longer recognize the bill originally passed, because it has been so much altered by public servants.
Madam Speaker, public servants disguise and systematically destroy our legislation. We, the representatives of the people can take any legislation and we will see what finally happens to it. Public servants, destroy, distort and systematically spoil the legislation by making regulations to annoy our fellow citizens. Paid by whom and how? God alone knows and perhaps also the minister. It is not sure and there is no proof of it. It appears in the bill: by-laws.
Well, Madam Speaker, I think that the officials must realize that it is very well to study the legislation, that it is very well to pass it, but those who will read Hansard tomorrow, must be aware whether they are French-speaking or English-speaking, from Quebec or British Columbia, that the members of this House intend to do their work and want to be equitably treated.
I am not speaking tonight to get a salary increase. The people know that I am in favour of it. I do not hide the fact. However, Madam Speaker, we have succeeded in bringing to a standstill that strong majority government which used to say: Give us a majority! They are there. They asked for a 50 per cent increase. Faced with NDP blackmailers and conniving reporters, they backed down to 30 per cent. Then, they retreated further still and today the same bill has been shelved because they are afraid of public opinion. Meanwhile what is that so-called strong majority government doing? Well, it is laughing at the members and introducing a bill to give unlimited powers enabling an internal committee to control broadcasting.
Madam Speaker, I think that the Liberal members are cowards and the servants of great financial interests-this is obvious-but in the case of public servants, it has now become a sure thing.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to make some comments at the end of today's debate on Bill C-5 which, for every member of Parliament, is nonetheless very important. We have been talking for a long time about the possibility to improve telecommunications, today we have before us a bill which provides for the establishment of a national commission responsible at the national level for everything related to communications.
As some of my colleagues of all parties, I have had the opportunity to make my views known to the responsible minister. First, I would like to say that I agree with some comments which have been made in this House on this bill. At the outset, I would like particularly to support my colleague, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner), who did make some appropriate comments this afternoon, particularly about Quebec. We know quite well that the respect of the provinces must be preserved. As for us, we regret and we condemn, in any case, and if I am to believe the comments made by the three opposition parties, I think that we severely condemn the government's centralizing policy in various fields.
Thus, last week, we examined Bill C-49, and we urged the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) to wait until after the meeting with the ministers responsible for taxation and especially royalties, which he refused to do. This

March 4, 1975
Broadcasting
meeting will of course take place after the decision was taken; we shall have a legislation which, once more, will be followed by a meeting of the provincial ministers of communications in a few weeks, and, once more, we have to take a decision before the meeting takes place. However, Madam Speaker, it seems to me that it would be so easy to wait until the results of the meeting are known, that it would be so easy to take advantage of this meeting to make a legislation which might meet, I say meet, Madam Speaker, the wishes of the provinces.
But no. Once again, the government quickens the pace and wants the legislation to be passed as quickly as possible. The provinces will be consulted later. They refuse to admit that these decisions are unilateral. Within a week, they will be talking once again of a viable, profitable federalism that is interesting for the provinces. And they want the provinces to be perfectly happy under our system which is frustrating for several of them.
This afternoon, Madam Speaker, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) talked about the position of the Quebec Minister of Communications. In the last two years, I think, the Quebec government has made representations on several occasions. It stated its position on communications. I heard some members, including my colleague on my left, who talked about respect for the provinces, about a policy geared to the needs and aspirations of the provinces. We want a legislation that would take national unity into account and, of course, we serve this cause by attacking all the problems we know of. How can we talk of national unity when we refuse to consider seriously the representations of the provinces?
It was clearly established that several provinces gave their support to the province of Quebec in a particular field called cablevision. We know perfectly, well that it is unthinkable to aim at national unity if we do not respect the wish of the provinces. And I wonder to what extent the present government is aware of the problem. On several occasions, Madam Speaker, I discussed with members of the opposition or even government members from Quebec who are certainly sensitive to the problems of their province and who felt the need to come and serve Quebec. But how can they serve it?
I heard my colleagues from other provinces who have that responsibility of meeting the aspirations of their provinces. We, of the Progressive Conservative Party, were being accused as recently as last week of having responded only to the Alberta proposal on the oil issue. Let me tell you, Madam Speaker, that this provides me with another opportunity to commend the people of Alberta for standing up for a natural resource within their own limits as recognized by the constitution.
Is it possible today in face of the legislation that was brought in to keep quiet and let the government introduce a bill to set up a national commission, to set up a national policy, knowing quite well that the government on several occasions recognized regional disparities, marked differences between areas and provinces? How can anyone think, whether it be in the area of energy with the people of Alberta or in the area of communications or cultural matters, of setting up a national policy that would meet

the aspirations of all Canadians without bearing consideration for the ethnic groups that make up this country and particularly the two founding groups? It is unthinkable, Madam Speaker. So they can talk to me of national harmony, a policy that could meet the aspirations of those founding groups, those ethnic groups, those provinces, those marked differences at the national level, and in the area of communications it's the same thing.
So, Madam Speaker, I would like to say this to respond in the affirmative to the government of Quebec that is not a government for which I worked on a regular basis, on the contrary. But I think my responsibility vis-a-vis my commitments prompts me to rise to the aspirations of my province, as the people of Alberta did so well to the aspirations of their province on the oil issue. Other provinces will also have to respond to their own needs, and I think in that way we can create a national harmony that will meet the objective we pursue of building a country in which there would be an understanding.
The Quebec provincial minister in charge of communications said two years ago, and repeated, the following: Quebec states it has exclusive jurisdiction in this area. Cable television is an undertaking of a local nature for the purposes of the British North America Act. It can be quite clearly identified geographically, contrary to airwaves, and we see no reason why it should be under federal responsibility. Of course the federal government feels cable TV is only an extension of radio and television broadcasting. We submit that contention does not hold. Because cable TV is essentially a means of communication, just as the telephone.
I believe every member realizes that this area in particular must meet the needs and mentality of a province or an area. The minister goes on to say:
It is currently used mainly to rebroadcast television programs. Cable television however will have in the years to come a very diversified range of applications going well beyond retransmission of TV programs. In that context, we see no reason to support federal reasoning in this area.
The Quebec minister in charge of communications further stated, and I quote:
As you may see, the Quebec government's view contradicts in no way the federal role in communications. It simply emphasizes that Canada is a federation comprised of eleven governments, which eleven governments have various substantial responsibilities in the field of communications. The situation would be very different if Canada were a centrally unified state. But such is not the case, for very precise reasons you are aware of. Since we live in a federation, each level of government must be allowed to truly fulfill its purposes. This in no way balkanizes Canada, notwithstanding claims to the contrary; quite the opposite, the eleven governments can very well agree on certain national criteria in the field of communications, which should become the parameters for a truly national communications policy; it would then be the responsibility of each government to implement that policy, within its own jurisdiction. In our opinion, it is not absolutely necessary that everything be centralized in Ottawa in the name of national unity which, in such a case, becomes instead national uniformity. In fact, we feel that Canada is not a uniform country, far from it, and that true national unity derives precisely from the promotion and vitality of its various cultures.
This is, Madam Speaker, what the Quebec minister responsible for communications was saying hardly a year ago. And since then, we are aware of the conflict between the federal and the Quebec governments, we also know that all provinces do not readily accept the federal government's propositions being made at this time.
Therefore, I am taking these few minutes, Madam Speaker, to urge the government to seriously consider the

problem, especially since it has about 60 members from Quebec. I think these members have a responsibility towards Quebec as the other members of other provinces have also towards their own province.
Could it be possible to believe that because of a party line, as representatives of a province, our interests and our responsibilities are betrayed? I venture to think it could not, Madam Speaker. In my opinion, the government of Quebec, not only through its Minister of Communications, but also in many other fields and for a number of years, has made representations to the federal government which unfortunately were not received as well as they should have been in this particular field, considering the peculiar situation of the province of Quebec.
I shall perhaps offend or irritate a few members. I think that we must recognize in this matter the particular position of the province of Quebec, and I challenge anybody to say anything to the contrary. The government members know what I mean. The government members will not dare say that I am wrong, Madam Speaker, but I should have liked them to take position and state that Quebec is wrong when it recommends privileged positions in communications, as Quebec is willing to acknowledge privileged positions for any English-speaking province, according to its needs, its mentality and its traditions.
Thus I think it is important to underline this aspect and I dare believe that the responsible French-speaking minister of Quebec will be able to meet the demands of the Quebec government and the wishes of a founding nation which does not hesitate to recognize the arguments put forward by the other provinces. I do not accept, Madam Speaker, that we be called separatists when we defend the interests of Quebec in this House or that the Quebec Minister of Communications be labelled a separatist when we defend him, because he deeply and sincerely meets a well-founded wish we have, as Quebecers.
All those who tried to call separatists the responsible minister or Quebecers who do not agree with a centralizing policy of the federal government are wrong. They are not necessarily separatists, but they have good intentions, they are deeply nationalistic, they surely believe in Canada and recognize the marked differences in this country. On behalf of these differences, on behalf of national harmony, we must thus search for much more than national unity. Mr. L'Allier rejects uniformity. I happen to be one of those who reject uniformity. I have respect for my colleagues and hope that we can find policies that will stick to the real facts and to the regional and provincial context, so that we can definitely speak, of a viable federalism.
Madam Speaker, we cannot otherwise believe in a viable federalism. Let us not ask ourselves any longer why, both in Quebec and in other provinces, problems add up every day, and why, particularly in Quebec, thousands of Quebecers have ceased to believe in federalism because of certain centralizing policies overlooking representations made by the provincial government and the context of important differences in Canada.
Madam Speaker, I conclude by saying that the minister could have waited till the meeting is held in a short time from now instead of putting immediately this bill before us. He could have discussed the matter once more, even if
Broadcasting
only to try one last time to give an affirmative and satisfactory answer to the Quebec government.
I have serious doubts that Quebec would be displeased with the communications policy. I shall never hesitate to live up to the aspirations of Quebec and I think this is the sacred duty, of every hon. member from that province. Of course, I do not want to be the only one to do so. It may be believed that we are fulfilling that obligation in a satisfactory way. I think that policy sufficiently important, and I know the minister well enough, Madam Speaker, to be familiar with his past record, truly in the Quebec spirit, to respect, to make the ultimate effort to fulfil that province's aspirations, as Quebecers are expecting it. I do hope that the minister will give us the replies we want.

I really cannot accept this statement, and I hope that we will have an occasion to explain what we have been doing. Had the hon. member only read the correspondence I tabled a few weeks ago in this very chamber, he would have known that his statement was incorrect.
If our Tory friends on the other side of the House are very concerned with financial inflation, they surely are not concerned very much-at least not the hon. member for Regina East-with verbal inflation. When he said, for instance, that the communications mess was crippling our country, I should say that the vigour of the argument has no equal, except perhaps the weakness of evidence, because he did not even try to say how communications are crippling this country. It is quite the contrary, when one thinks that we have one of the best telephone systems in the whole world, that we have the first domestic communications satellite system and one of the most advanced systems of computer communications.
The hon. member is just satisfied to say that a communications mess is crippling our country, without giving any evidence, and he would have to be a little more logical than that. At least he should state some facts, in committee or somewhere else, if he wants to persuade anyone including, I suspect, himself. The most dangerous comment that he made is that this bill is presented to the House without the consent of the provinces. This goes as well for the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) who obviously was talking through his hat.

speechtext:
At the first conference more than a year ago, I told all the provinces that this bill would be presented and that it would not change anything except to tidy up the system and join two existing regulatory bodies. No province made any objection to our presenting what we called in the department and in our talks with the provinces the first phase of the legislation. Not one province objected to that. They all admitted this was a housekeeping operation on the part of the federal government. If hon. members had read the bill carefully they would have seen it applies only to federally regulated societies, corporations, agencies and what-not. So, this is not done without their consent and we have nothing to wait for in this case. Not one province objected to our presenting this legislation at this time.
I do not have much to say about the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) except that his denunciation of the CTC lacked a foundation in evidence, and some of his rhetorical questions had already been answered before he asked them in his speech. He asked, for instance, where the government stands on the indexing of telephone rates of Bell Canada. The position of the government was put clearly. Perhaps he was on holiday and did not get the press release. The statement I made, after there had been a cabinet decision, was clear. It was that the government was not espousing this position but that it would not stifle the discussion of any question, including that one, by the CTC. He wondered what is the position of the CTC. Let him wait. The hearings are just starting and every intervener will be in the position to make his case. Only after that has been done will the CTC express an opinion, because it will genuinely try to explore a question and find a satisfying answer. [Translation]
Let me now quickly come to the remarks of the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner). He too indulges in verbal inflation when he says that nothing was undertaken since 1963 to develop the technology of communications in Canada. The only thing I can say is that the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe just did not keep abreast of progress in that field. He too does not know what the development of computer-communications was, and I could brief him if ever he can spare the time. He too omits Telesat Canada which is a world premiere for our country. He also forgets about a lot of progress made with respect to the use of cable, television and broadcasting, and his assertion is senseless. But another remark by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe baffles me even more, and we cannot get on with the debate on that bill without challenging such a statement. The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe says: According to the CRTC, the cable would be under federal jurisdiction. The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe has only been a short time in this Parliament, because if he had been here in 1969, he would have realized that no jurisdictional powers were granted by the CRTC but through the act, which as a matter of fact was upheld everytime there was an appeal against it since it was passed.
Such a decision did not originate in the CRTC, but in Parliament, which the hon. member for Saint Hyacinthe is a member of, maybe not for very long, but nevertheless a

member of. He should realize, and so should the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. LaSalle) as well, that the argument he is talking about was not started by the federal government against the provincial government, but that the provincial government of Quebec did so by trespassing on a jurisdiction which every court decision acknowledged to be a federal one, by passing an act whose provisions are still being challenged in courts, since that act was passed without any consultation with the federal government.
And when the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe put forward the testimony of Mr. Henderson against the federal jurisdiction with respect to communications, I wonder if he realizes that his source was the great supporter of American interests versus Canadian broadcasting in a recent case before the federal court.
In connection with the remarks made by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin), Madam Speaker, I merely want to say that I never saw a man breaking down an open door with such vigour. He said that we are setting up a new agency. He did not read the bill. In fact, we are making one out of two. We are not setting up a new one. Because we are combining two agencies, there will be one less, according to my calculations. I do not know where the hon. member learned his arithmetic. He also finds it shocking that the bill should mention the setting up of a regulatory body before setting forth its responsibilities.
Madam Speaker, I wonder if the hon. member has any spare time. Since 1969 and even 1967, he should have spent a little time reading the Broadcasting Act which is still in force and sets forth, in Part II, all the responsibilities and functions of this body, In a bill aimed at combining two regulatory agencies, we were not going to include each and every section of the Broadcasting Act. May I suggest to the hon. member to refer to Part II of the Broadcasting Act which was adopted in 1967. He had eight years to read it, which gave him ample time, it seems to me. He would find in it everything he was shocked not to find in the bill before us tonight.
As to the salaries of MPs, I must say that I somewhat agree with him, although I do not quite see how it is relevant to this debate. On the broadcasting issue, however, I must say that he broke down an open door, but luckily for him, it was not an open window because we would have lost him for future debates.
Madam Speaker, that sums up my remarks. I thank all the members who took part in this debate. I believe we will be able to clarify many questions, some of which were most relevant, put by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes), in committee as well as during the subsequent stages this bill will go through.

subtopic: BILINGUALISM-POSSIBILITY OF FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO GROUPS CONTESTING CONSTITUTIONALITY OF BILL 22

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: BILINGUALISM-POSSIBILITY OF FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO GROUPS CONTESTING CONSTITUTIONALITY OF BILL 22
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who, if he is anything at all, ought to be the keeper of the constitution of this country, said that he will not initiate any action to bring Quebec's Bill 22 before the Supreme Court of Canada.
Bill 22, no matter from what end it is viewed, is perhaps the most divisive piece of legislation that has ever appeared on a federal or provincial statute book. Quite aside from the fact that it was rammed through the

March 4, 1975
Adjournment Debate
Quebec assembly, it makes a mockery of the official languages policy of the federal government. It is a denial of justice to the English speaking minority in Quebec and to those who came to Canada from other parts of the world.
There are aspects of the bill about which there can be a real question as to their constitutionality. Basically, it is an attempt by a provincial government to amend the British North America Act. It has a profound effect on the rights of Canadians to learn and to have their children taught in the language of their choice. In the long run it will do more to damage the relationship in our country between the two major language groups than anything that has preceded it.
The bill places an astounding reliance on bureaucrats, a state of affairs that is questionable in itself. Rule by regulation is the order of the day. I cannot imagine anything more dangerous where basic rights are seen to be threatened. However, what does the Prime Minister do? First, he will not disallow the bill. He used as his excuse that the remedy of disallowance has not been used for 30 years. Perhaps that is a greater tribute to the wisdom of provincial governments than an indication of the obsolescence of the method.
The Prime Minister was asked if the federal government would refer the matter to the Supreme Court of Canada so that this smouldering time-bomb could be laid to rest one way or another. The terror of the fund-raising dinner in Montreal is not such a terror after all. He refused to do that. I then asked him the question which is the subject of this debate tonight. In effect, he does not have the courage to take action himself and so he hides behind other groups.
I asked the Prime Minister whether he would aid financially those who do in fact have that courage. He did it with the Indians in James Bay. However, again the great leader evaded, slithered and slid away. In the House he stated it would be considered, but outside the House he is reported to have said in effect that no one ought to hold their breath. Those who paid $125 to attend his fund raising dinner should ask to have their money refunded.
When asked what instructions would be given to federal counsel intervening in a private action, he avoided answering the question. He called it hypothetical. Well, Madam Speaker, Bill 22 is not hypothetical. It is a reality. The problems are real. The people it affects are real. Its authoritative power is real. Its divisive quality is real indeed. In the judgment of many, it is a blot on the legislative landscape of this country. It ought to be dealt with swiftly and finally, and not allowed to linger and fester as an irritant to confederation. I have to confess that I am left with more than a lingering doubt about the political courage of the Prime Minister when he deals with the government of Quebec.
I have not met any right-thinking person who does not have a sympathetic understanding of or desire to see the French language and the French culture survive in Canada, but surely no one can agree that this ought to be at the expense of the rights of others. That is what the reaction to this bill is all about. The bill should be tested, and tested immediately, so that the question can be laid to rest, and the Prime Minister ought not hide behind the skirts of others to bring this about.

speakeroldname: Mr. John M. Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BILINGUALISM-POSSIBILITY OF FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO GROUPS CONTESTING CONSTITUTIONALITY OF BILL 22
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Canadian constitution makes it quite clear that the responsibility for passing this kind of legislation belongs to the government of Quebec, not to the government of Canada. The government of Quebec was elected in a democratic election, with one of the largest majorities that has been seen in modern Canadian political history. It is, therefore, obvious that it is acting within its legislative competence.
To deal with the other argument concerning whether the federal government ought to interfere, I would point out to the hon. member that the constitutional foundations of the legislation are apparently well based. Even more important, the basis on which that act is based is the Manitoba Act, passed in 1892 by the government of Manitoba, which at that time could not be accused of racism, at least as against English speaking people.
The government of Canada does have and does acknowledge a special responsibility toward the Indians in Quebec, particularly the James Bay Indians. Under Section 91 of the constitution of Canada, the British North America Act, the government of Canada does indeed have a special responsibility. Even more important is the fact that when the land in question was transferred to the government of Quebec in 1912, the government of Quebec did not come to a settlement with the Indians in the north. Thus, in addition to the general responsibility of the government of Canada toward the Indians of James Bay there is a particular responsibility because no land settlement had been made. It seems to me the hon. gentleman is trying to bring in through the back door of parliament something he could not bring in through the front door, namely, to argue a Quebec matter.

subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-USE OF BURWASH INDUSTRIAL FARM AS MEDIUM SECURITY INSTITUTION
PENITENTIARIES-USE OF BURWASH INDUSTRIAL FARM AS MEDIUM SECURITY INSTITUTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on February 14 I asked the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) whether he would consider upgrading the Burwash Institution at Nickel Belt to medium security status rather than spend $7 million on building a new medium security prison somewhere near Barrie. I pointed out to the minister that 200 jobs representing a $2 million payroll to the Sudbury region would be lost to northeastern Ontario. The minister's reply was very interesting and I should like to quote it:
We have already examined this possibility with the government of Ontario. Unfortunately, it does not seem that the Burwash Institution would be satisfactory for federal needs. First of all, our policy now is to move into smaller institutions which accommodate 150 to 180 inmates. Second, we try to locate the institutions as near as possible to the major population areas from which inmates come. Our need is in southern Ontario and not in northern Ontario, because most of the inmates come from southern Ontario. For these reasons we do not feel that Burwash is suitable at the present time.
Let me deal with the first point the minister made-I am positive the parliamentary secretary will make it again tonight, namely, that the present policy is to move into smaller institutions which accommodate 150 to 180 inmates. First, let me point out that facilities at Burwash are located in three camps. The most appropriate, meeting

the department's new policy, is Camp Bison, which houses between 180 and 200 prisoners.
The minister's observation that Burwash is a rather large institution requiring a lot of work and great expense indicates that he is not aware of the situation. Yes, the Burwash Camp is old and decrepit and ought to be torn down. But the Bison Camp has excellent facilities. The provincial government has spent around $4 million over the last four years in improving those facilities. First, it built a new gymnasium at a cost of $1 million-it was opened in October, 1971. Then it built a sports building complex for $40,000, a bridge at the Bison Camp for $5,000, and a new staff quarters, constructed in 1973, for $500,000. Road servicing in the settlement cost $30,000, and an inmate visiting room was provided for $350,000.
The provincial government built an entirely new sewage complex for $1 million, and made renovations to employee homes at the settlement costing $250,000. Brand new housing for single male guards and new homes for employees accounted for a further $200,000, and it even put in a new floor in the main prison for $4,000. The Bell Telephone Company put in new cables and connections at a cost of $40,000, and an entirely new plate shop, garage and laundry were provided for a further $1 million. Heating of living units was converted from coal to oil in 1972. Indeed it also laid a new main steam pipe for $95,000, and renovated homes to provide accommodation for guards-two apartments per home-which were finished. The camp then closed and they were never occupied.
The second argument that the minister proposes is that the new policy is to locate institutions as near as possible to major population centres from which the inmates come. I would point out that Burwash is near Sudbury, North Bay, Manitoulin Island, Parry Sound, etc., and one should note that the population in this area is between 200,000 and 350,000 people. Surely this is a large enough population area.
Moreover, if the minister is sincere about closeness to the homes of the prisoners, what about those prisoners from Sudbury and surrounding districts? Obviously they are going to be rehabilitated away from the areas where they grew up if the new prison is built somewhere in southern Ontario.
The third point I should like to make, Madam Speaker, is the economic one. Burwash was the fourth largest secondary industry in the Sudbury area, and when it closed it took a severe toll on the economic life of small communities near the prison, communities such as Estaire. Property values are down 50 per cent from a year ago, and small businesses have been forced to close.
It is also of interest to point out that the people who live around the Burwash prison settlement are accustomed to the prison being within the precincts of their community and have never viewed the prisoners with any kind of distaste, or adopted an arm's length approach. I understand that in the Barrie area, where the new prison is being concentrated, many communities are up in arms at the fact that prisoners are being brought into their community.
When I listen to ministers of the government talking so sanctimoniously about wanting to develop those parts of
Adjournment Debate
our country that lack secondary industry and about the diversification of job opportunities, when I hear them talking about discouraging people from living in large urban centres, and when I witness decisions being made to create more jobs in large urban centres near Toronto, then I know they are either mad or hypocritical, or both.
The fact of the matter is that Camp Bison can easily be converted into a medium security prison for approximately 180 prisoners at a cost far less than $7 million of the taxpayers' money. Jobs will come to the Sudbury district. The prisoners will be close to a large urban centre, Sudbury, consisting pf 90,000 persons, and which offers a university community college, several large athletic facilities and three very good hospitals.
Once again I urge the minister to review this decision. If he wishes he can send his officials to investigate the facility that I have described tonight. I am quite prepared to accompany them on such a visit. I ask him to revise the decision that has been made and to take advantage of the Camp Bison facility to establish a medium security prison in our part of the country.

speakeroldname: Mr. John M. Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-USE OF BURWASH INDUSTRIAL FARM AS MEDIUM SECURITY INSTITUTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) has made a powerful argument for the province of Ontario to reopen the Burwash Industrial Farm. He has indicated the amount of money that the province of Ontario has recently invested in this facility, and I think his case is certainly convincing that the provincial government ought to reopen the farm. However, he has not made the case that the federal government ought to take over the facility.
The Canadian penitentiary service has examined this possibility following an offer from the province of Ontario to sell the institution. Unfortunately its conclusion has been that Burwash would not be satisfactory for federal penitentiary needs.
It is now the policy, as the hon. member has indicated, that the Canadian penitentiary service should move into smaller institutions which will accommodate no more than 150 to 180 inmates. The service attempts to locate these institutions as close as possible to the major population centres from which the inmates come. I should point out to the hon. member for Nickel Belt, who like me is a member from northern Ontario, that our population is peace loving, does not get into trouble or require the utilization of the aforementioned service. The need for such services tends to be much more prevalent among those who come from larger centres in the industrialized east. I am sure many eastern members here would agree with those comments.
In any event, the other factor of considerable importance is the resocialization process which has now become a great part of the penitentiary service and which involves renewing or maintaining close family relationships, which are again facilitated by placing the prisoners in centres near their homes.
It is now the policy of the Canadian penitentiary service to house inmates of maximum, medium and minimum security risk in different institutions. Based on a study of

inmates' places of origin, it has been established that the need for federal institutions is in southern Ontario and not in the northern part of the province, for some of the reasons I gave previously.
However, following the study made by the penitentiary service regarding the possible use of Burwash, it was established that remodelling older existing facilities to meet current requirements could be just as expensive as building new facilities. If the alternative of remodelling Burwash had been accepted because of financial considerations, the location would still have been unsatisfactory.
Consequently, and after due consideration of the economic implications of the closing of this institution by the government of the province of Ontario, it has been agreed that in the best interests of the Canadian penitentiary service, its staff and particularly the inmates for which it is responsible, it was necessary to build the type of institution required closer to the geographical areas where such facilities are needed.
