subtopic: AGRICULTURE-INEQUITY BETWEEN TARIFF ON IMPORTED CHEESE AND CANADIAN CHEESE IMPORTED BY EUROPEAN COMMON MARKET
AGRICULTURE-INEQUITY BETWEEN TARIFF ON IMPORTED CHEESE AND CANADIAN CHEESE IMPORTED BY EUROPEAN COMMON MARKET
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on February 6 as recorded at page 2967 of Hansard I asked questions of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) regarding the Canadian cheese industry. In doing so I pointed out that Canadian cheddar, which previously was exported to European Common Market countries in large quantity, was now facing EEC import duties of about 65 cents a pound, indeed as high as 67 cents. Therefore the volume of these cheddar exports had slowed down to a trickle.
At the same time I also pointed out to the minister that European soft cheeses were coming into Canada in large volume because our import duties, rather than being 65 cents or 67 cents a pound, were only one cent to three and a half cents per pound.
On February 6 I asked the minister what he was going to do about this apparent gross inequity. I pointed out that many Canadian cheese producers, because they are on a quota system for cheddar production, also produce specialty or soft cheeses, and the sales of these cheeses in the Canadian market have dropped drastically in volume, by as much as 25 per cent to 30 per cent in the last two months because of the inability of Canadian producers to compete with European imports in the specialty cheese market. On February 6 the minister indicated that the matter would be reviewed.
Yesterday in the House of Commons, as reported at page 3712 of Hansard, I asked the minister whether the matter had been reviewed and what action, if any, was being taken. The minister told us that the matter was going to be discussed in cabinet in a few days.

Later during the question period yesterday the minister decided to be a little more frank with us and announced, as recorded at page 3715, that an agreement had been reached so that commencing in April and continuing until 1979 our cheddar will be allowed into the EEC without import duty. This is welcome news, not only for cheese producers but also, I suggest, for Europeans who will be able to consume the finest cheese in the world, hopefully at reasonable prices.
Unfortunately the minister did not tell us about the fate of Canadian produced specialty or soft cheeses which cannot compete here in Canada with European imports. One might be tempted to ask whether our cheese producers are less efficient than their European counterparts, but this is not the case.
What is happening is simply that European governments are paying subsidies to their cheese producers who export to Canada. Therefore Canadians must not only compete with European cheese makers, they must also attempt to compete with subsidies paid by foreign governments. I trust the minister realizes how difficult, if not impossible, is this type of competition.
I cannot emphasize too much the importance of these Canadian specialty cheeses. Generally they are produced by small companies in rural areas. In other words, I am not talking about the large companies such as Kraft. I am trying to speak for the small cheese plants throughout our country.
In Ontario, for example, a typical cheese plant cannot operate at a sufficient percentage of its capacity to be profitable if it produces only cheddar. This is because of the Ontario quota system which restricts cheddar production. In order to be efficient these small plants developed good and nourishing specialty cheeses. They made substantial investments in capital equipment and they marketed their products successfully, all without government help. As a result their plants were profitable and they provided employment in our rural areas. Now they find themselves in the serious position of not being able to compete with foreign products which have the unfair advantage of lower prices because of a foreign government subsidy.
Therefore, while I welcome the news about the lifting of European Common Market import duties on our cheddar, I cannot help but be extremely concerned about the other factor that is essential to the viability of an average small cheese plant, and that is the necessity of being able to market its Canadian specialty cheeses. It is important to realize that such plants in many cases rely on the production of both types of cheese to keep their facilities in operration. In other words, many plants would operate at a loss if they were restricted to cheddar production only.
What is particularly disturbing to me are recent news reports which indicate that it may take some time before this problem is resolved. I refer the minister to a recent feature article by James Rush in the Toronto Globe and Mail of February 26. One paragraph reads as follows:
Canadian officials, however, warn that, confident as they are that some accommodation will be worked out with the community (EEC) it could still take some months to resolve the situation.
If this is an accurate view, and I have no reason to doubt that it is, there are in my opinion two danger signals. First
March 4, 1975

is the time that our officials seem to feel that it will take to work out the problem. This raises the simple question, can many of our cheese plants operate in a loss position for this period of time? Second, I would hope that our government is not concerning itself simply with the Cheddar problem to the exclusion of the specialty cheese problem. I suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that the viability of many plants depends on the production of both products.
The minister is not one who is opposed to normal free trade. I point out to him, Mr. Speaker, that when a foreign government subsidizes one of its products which it is exporting to Canada, that is not free trade in the sense I understand free trade.
Third, we have had a history in certain agricultural production of cutting off our nose to spite our face. In other words, we accepted the importation of foreign products. Canadian producers could not compete with these imports and were forced out of business. One might say this was fair to the consumer. We might say a consumer is entitled to the best deal he can get in buying a certain product, whether it is produced in Canada or elsewhere. But, in the long run, it has been the consumer who has suffered, because as soon as there is no Canadian production to compete with the foreign product, the price of the foreign product goes way up and the consumer pays the inflated price. I use as obvious examples the following: the wool industry, the baler twine industry and the sugar beet industry. I only urge that the minister does not allow the Canadian cheese industry to suffer the unhappy fate of these examples I have just mentioned.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-INEQUITY BETWEEN TARIFF ON IMPORTED CHEESE AND CANADIAN CHEESE IMPORTED BY EUROPEAN COMMON MARKET
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to deal with two points raised by the hon. member, the question of imported cheeses for further processing and the cheddar cheese situation.
Since 1970 the government has maintained controls on imports of cheese for further processing to deal with a threat of disruption of the Canadian industry. At present no cheese for processing is allowed to enter the country with the exception of a small quantity from Finland, based on their traditional trade which existed before 1970.
Adjournment Debate
Cheese for direct consumption, except cheddar and colby, has been allowed to enter freely under general import permit. There have recently been suggestions that some cheese ostensibly imported for direct consumption has in fact been finding its way into processing. We are at present urgently looking into what can be done to correct this situation. When a decision has been reached the House will be informed.
I should like to elaborate a little on the cheddar cheese situation and the outcome of the successful negotiations with the European Economic Community, negotiations which were triggered by the enlargement of the EEC by the British, Danish and Irish entries, in respect of compensation for the impairment of our trading rights. These were conducted under Article XXIV:6. As the hon. member indicated, there were substantial benefits negotiated.
This arrangement applies to aged Canadian cheddar cheese which meets certain agreed price and quality specifications. A fixed levy will amount to 15 EEC units of account per 100 kilograms, just under 8V4 cents per pound at present exchange rates. This represents a big reduction from the current basic EEC levy of 112 units of account per 100 kilograms, or approximately 67 cents per pound.
Because EEC levies are being phased in in Britain over a transitional period, the result of our special arrangement will be that no levy will apply at first, and a full levy of 15 units of account will not come into effect until 1979.
The effective date of arrangement is April 1, 1975. The trade will shortly be provided with full details of the way in which it will operate. The British market has traditionally been of major importance to Canadian cheese producers. During the period 1963 to 1972 annual exports to Britain amounted to some 28 million pounds, approximately $11.2 million in value terms. This represented about 95 per cent of total Canadian cheddar exports. Virtually no Canadian cheese has been exported to Britain since the application of the EEC variable levies two years ago.
Hon. members will recognize the important benefits negotiated by the government.
